articles.title: Supreme Court revives controversial US data system for citizenship checks
articles.summary: The system uses citizenship information and other sensitive data to filter alleged non-citizen voting.

blocks.text: The US Supreme Court has lifted restrictions on the Trump administration to use a controversial federal voter database, which uses citizenship information and other sensitive data to filter alleged non-citizen voting.
Critics warn the ruling could lead to valid voters being removed from electoral rolls.
The ruling marks a victory for the Trump administration as it seeks to clamp down on allegations of non-citizen voting.

The three liberal-leaning liberals on the Supreme Court dissented from the decision, with the other six conservative justices supporting it. In June, a federal judge ruled that the system was illegal and violated the privacy rights of Americans.
The Department of Homeland Security programme, known as Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements, or SAVE, allows officials to verify the eligibility of voters on their rolls.

The database was first created in 1986 to help officials verify the citizenship or immigration status of those applying for public benefits. But the Trump administration last year expanded its search capabilities by allowing bulk searches using social security numbers.

In June, however, US District Judge Sparkle L Soonnan - a Biden-appointee - ruled that the revamped system shows that the federal government "knowingly trampled on the privacy rights" of US citizens "in a manner that threatens the sacred right to vote."
A federal appeals court allowed her ruling to stand, only to be overridden by the Supreme Court on Friday.

articles.title: Healey appoints Labour manifesto writer, adding to election speculation
articles.summary: Exclusive: Economist Ravinder Athwal, who worked in Keir Starmer’s team, is poached from Flint Global

blocks.text: Ravinder Athwal, the economist who wrote Labour’s 2024 manifesto, is taking on a senior role as an adviser to John Healey, in a move likely to fuel speculation about an early general election.
The chancellor is keen to strengthen his team before the critical budget on 28 October, as the economy is buffeted by high oil prices and rising government borrowing costs.

Healey has poached Athwal to be his senior special adviser from the business advisory group Flint Global, previously run by Andy Burnham’s chief of staff, the former Blair-era cabinet minister James Purnell.

Athwal, a Cambridge economics graduate, was closely associated with drawing up Labour’s manifesto, and devising Keir Starmer’s five “missions”, which were meant to shape Labour’s approach to government. He worked as a senior economic adviser in Starmer’s Downing Street team but left after a year to join Flint Global.

A source close to Healey said: “Having Rav join John’s team as an experienced heavyweight economist at the Treasury ahead of this budget will be invaluable. His political nous will add to the special adviser team, providing John with guidance and counsel to the chancellor.”

Burnham flatly denied that he planned to call an early election on Friday. Asked by ITV Calendar whether the next general election would be in 2029, he said, “well, yes, that’s when the next election will be. All of this speculation on an early election, I can knock that dead.”
Nevertheless, Athwal’s presence on Healey’s team could be seen as a strength if the prime minister did decide to draw up a fresh manifesto.
Athwal’s arrival is also likely to increase concerns among some in Labour that the Treasury’s instinctive caution is fuelling a “continuity Starmer” approach to economics.

The pledge at the heart of the manifesto not to increase income tax, national insurance or VAT was seen by Starmer’s team as key to Labour’s landslide victory two years ago. But it is widely agreed that it has restricted the party’s room for manoeuvre once in power.

People with knowledge of Athwal’s thinking suggest he has learned from the travails of Labour’s early months in office, however. One left-of-centre economist said: “I’d say he was at the more interesting and curious end of the Starmerite project.”
Before joining Labour, Athwal was a Treasury civil servant, rising to be head of growth strategy. One former colleague described him as “nice and clever – a good combination”.

After taking over at the Treasury in July, Healey hired Will Straw, who played a leading role in the remain campaign during the Brexit referendum, to be his chief of staff; some of Rachel Reeves’s economic advisers, including Spencer Thompson, stayed on.

Reeves’s chief economic adviser, the former Clean Bandit violinist Neil Amin-Smith, who was closely involved in her plans to devolve more tax revenue to local leaders, has moved across to Burnham’s No 10.
Athwal is expected to arrive in post next week, a month before Healey’s first budget.
after newsletter promotion
With inflation and borrowing costs expected to have wiped out at least half of the headroom Reeves had built up against Labour’s fiscal rules, Healey faces a series of tough decisions.
He has promised to maintain a “buffer against uncertainty” but this is widely expected to be significantly smaller than the £24bn in the spring forecast.

Depending on the Office for Budget Responsibility’s forecasts, restoring the cushion in full would be likely to require large tax rises or spending cuts. But government sources say Healey wants this to be a “focused” budget, after Reeves used her two budgets as chancellor to increase taxes by £70bn a year.

Key decisions about future tax and spending appear likely to be delayed until a Treasury spending review next year, which will come after Burnham has set out his long-term priorities in a 10-year plan, expected after the budget.

Healey has made clear he does not intend to set a timetable for when the UK will spend 3% of gross domestic product on defence at the budget, for example – a target he insisted, when he resigned from Starmer’s government in June, must be met by 2030.

However, hopes of a low-key budget are under pressure from persistently high global oil and gas prices, which make it likely that the energy price cap, which determines UK consumer bills, will rise sharply in January.
Treasury sources have said officials are working “at pace” on options for consumer support, though help is expected to fall far short of the costly universal approach taken by Liz Truss in 2022.
Flint Global was approached for comment.

articles.title: Alberta’s ‘rat patrol’ ramps up operations as vermin makes inroads in province
articles.summary:
‘Rat-free’ Canadian province recently took a verminous hit when a dead rodent turned up in town of Bowden

For more than seven decades, residents of Alberta have shared something in common…

blocks.text: For more than seven decades, residents of Alberta have shared something in common with Antarctica and the high Arctic: all locations are officially free of rats.

But on Thursday the Canadian province’s reputation as a firewall against rodent infestation took a hit when the town of Bowden announced the discovery of a dead rat and called on the province’s “rat patrol” to investigate.
“If you’ve noticed rat droppings or any signs of rats, please contact Rat Patrol Alberta so they can follow up,” the town said in a statement. “Please stay alert and report any sightings.”
Officials in Bowden did not say where in the town the rat was found.

But as global temperatures increase, rat numbers have surged in major cities. Over the past decade, rats increased by 390% in Washington DC, 300% in San Francisco and 162% in New York, according to researchers, who analysed public sightings and infestation reports. Toronto, Canada’s largest city, is facing a “perfect rat storm”, with numbers up 186% in the last 10 years.
Unlike other regions in the world that have been overrun by the wily and adaptable urban mammals, Alberta has actively fought rats from entering at all.
“Albertans have enjoyed living without the menace of rats since 1950 when the Rat Control Program was established,” the province says in its rat guide.

It cites both the province’s unique geography, with mountain ranges and boreal forest surrounding most of Alberta, and the fact that the Norway rat – “one of the most destructive creatures known to man”, the province claims – cannot survive in vast natural areas and cannot overwinter in cultivated fields. The very lack of the humans and their structures that rats need to survive has given the province a chance to ward off infestation.

In the 1950s, suspecting rats might try to enter from the east by way of neighbouring Saskatchewan, Alberta officials created a “rat control zone” – a strip of land measuring 373 miles by 18 miles (600km by 30km) – to monitor incursions that ranges from Cold Lake in the north to the Montana border in the south.
In addition, from June 1952 to July 1953, 140,000lb of 73% arsenic trioxide powder was used to treat 8,000 buildings on 2,700 farms to slow the spread of rats.

The province also amended the Agricultural Pests Act of Alberta in 1950, obliging “every person and municipality” to destroy rats they found; made posters reminiscent of a national war effort; and hosted a radio show, Call of the Land, to educate residents.
Today, there are dedicated telephone lines and an email address to report rats.
But while the rat patrol receives hundreds of calls each year, it says the vast majority are not rats but muskrats, voles and field mice.

Still, it concedes there are exceptions. “Alberta’s rat-free status means there is no resident population of rats and they are not allowed to establish themselves. It does not mean we never get rats.”

articles.title: CBCP calls for passage of anti-dynasty law
articles.summary: The Catholic Bishops" Conference of the Philippines (CBCP) on Friday expressed support for the “Dapat Isa Lang” People"s Initiative, which seeks to pass an anti-political dynasty law, calling it a…

blocks.text: Published September 26, 2026 12:32am

The Catholic Bishops’ Conference of the Philippines (CBCP) on Friday expressed support for the “Dapat Isa Lang” People’s Initiative seeking the passage of an anti-political dynasty law, calling it a peaceful and democratic effort to fulfill a constitutional mandate.

In a pastoral statement signed by CBCP president Archbishop Gilbert Garcera, the bishops said political power should not become a “family inheritance” and stressed that public office is a public trust.

The CBCP said the 1987 Constitution calls for equal access to opportunities for public service and prohibits political dynasties as may be defined by law. Nearly 40 years after the Constitution was adopted, however, Congress has yet to enact an anti-political dynasty law.

"After almost forty years, the constitutional command against political dynasties should no longer remain merely an aspiration. The time has come to give it genuine meaning in law and in political life," it said.
The bishops said that their position was not directed against any particular political family, party, candidate or public official.

"The issue is not the goodness or competence of individual persons or families. The deeper concern is a system that allows political power to concentrate and be repeatedly passed among members of the same families, narrowing opportunities for other qualified citizens, weakening genuine political competition, and making accountability more difficult," the CBCP said.

"No family, however capable or respected, has a permanent claim to public office. Political leadership should remain open to all Filipinos who possess the competence, integrity, and desire to serve," it added.

It encouraged dioceses, parishes, Catholic schools and universities, religious communities and lay organizations to help the public understand the initiative and participate in the process through respectful dialogue and responsible information.
In particular, it rallied support for Dapat Isa Lang People's Initiative, "an exercise of the sovereignty that our Constitution recognizes as residing in the Filipino people."

Dapat Isa Lang was launched as a signature campaign in May this year aiming to gather at least seven million signatures —or 10 percent of the country's registered voters —to be able to pass a genuine anti-political dynasty law.

Early this week, the Supreme Court issued a decision compelling Congress to enact an appropriate anti-political dynasty law at the earliest opportunity. The high court added, “certain circumstances can be considered if the evils of concentrating power and political opportunity were to be truly addressed.”
Still, the SC said the High Tribunal “will not instruct on how the legislation will be crafted and how the scope and extent of the prohibition will be defined.” —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Novelist accused of using AI to write book removed from French prize list
articles.summary:
Thélyson Orélien had been in the running to win a top literary prize before the AI claim emerged on social media

The organisers of France’s most prestigious literary prize said they had…

blocks.text: The organisers of France’s most prestigious literary prize said they had removed a critically acclaimed novel by a Canadian-Haitian writer from the longlist after an anonymous online account claimed the book was “almost entirely” written by AI.

The Académie Goncourt, a Paris-based literary organisation, said on Friday its decision to withdraw Thélyson Orélien’s novel C’était ça ou mourir (It Was That or Die) was “driven by the desire to preserve the integrity of the Goncourt prize and the academy itself, whose central role is to promote and honour literature written by women and men”.

The Haiti-born author’s book is a lyrical first-person account of how a history and geography teacher flees a home country mired in gang violence and embarks on a perilous journey across 12 countries before finding a haven in Canada.
Published in France by Grasset in August, it has sold about 35,000 copies and won the Prix du roman Fnac, with translation rights sold to more than 20 countries.

blocks.caption: The novel on display inside a bookstore in Paris. Photograph: Sarah Meyssonnier/Reuters

blocks.text: Allegations that the book was written using AI emerged on X on 21 September, the same day It Was That or Die won the Fnac prize for best novel.

An anonymous account called Balance ton Claude – a reference to Anthropic’s AI agent – said it had fed the novel into the AI detection software Pangram and found it to be “almost entirely” written by artificial intelligence.
Questions have been raised over Pangram’s accuracy, and French media outlets have found other AI detection programmes that identified It Was That or Die as very probably written by a human.
Orélien, 38, has denied the allegation, saying it was racially motivated. “I’ve always loved creating and writing,” he said. “I don’t see why I would use a machine.”
He told the newspaper Libération that he used traditional language and rhythms that were Haitian and Caribbean. “The imagery, repetition and rhythm are a living language, they are mine.”

blocks.caption: Orélien at Les Correspondances literature festival in Manosque this week. Photograph: Joel Saget/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The author of the anonymous X account was later identified on the pages of the centre-right newspaper Le Figaro as one of its own columnists, Samuel Fitoussi, the author of an essay against “wokism” on film and TV.
On his own X account, Fitoussi said he had initiated his campaign because even though he was “techno-optimistic”, he feared that “AI will cause the disappearance of reading and writing”.

On Wednesday Philippe Claudel, the Académie Goncourt’s president, had urged “caution” over the allegations. But separate accusations of plagiarism against Orélien published in French media appeared to have caused a change of heart.

Libération alleged in an article that the author plagiarised an award-winning short story from the preface of the French journalist Louis Pauwels’ book The Morning of the Magicians, originally published in 1960.
after newsletter promotion

In its statement the academy referred to the “plagiarisms of which its author has been guilty over time and which have just been revealed, as well as the convergent result of several analyses by trustworthy researchers and journalists highlighting the fact that [the book] is in all likelihood very largely the product of artificial intelligence”.
“The aim is to send a clear message,” it added, “to affirm that we neither endorse nor condone in any way the creation of texts generated with the help of AI.”

In a statement shared with the Guardian, the novel’s original publisher, Le Éditions du Boréal, said: “Unfortunately, at this stage, we are unable to confirm or deny the allegations the author is facing.”
The Canada-based publisher said it was important not to “jump to conclusions”, adding: “Without credible, concrete evidence, it is not our place to decide whether this book has a right to exist.”

Boréal said it was “concerned” about the newer plagiarism allegations, but added it was important to remember there was a real person behind the book. “We unequivocally condemn the hateful messages and personal attacks of recent days, and we urge everyone to show restraint,” it said.

Orélien has said he will not comment further on the latest allegations. Speaking on Thursday at Les Correspondances literary festival in Manosque, southern France, he said: “There’s this desire not only to attack the book, but especially my voice … to silence me”, adding that he would therefore “take a step back and wait until things have calmed down”.
The Académie Goncourt will publish its shortlist on 6 October and announce the winner of the prize on 4 November.

articles.title: Pope Leo warns of AI threat to humanity at start of three-day France visit
articles.summary:
Pontiff says artificial intelligence must remain at service of people in first official papal visit to country in 18 years

Pope…

blocks.text: Pope Leo has warned against losing humanity in a “paradise of machines” as he addressed global concerns over the dangers of artificial intelligence at the start of a three-day visit to France.

“If we are to avoid losing our humanity amid a paradise of machines invading and conditioning our daily lives, there is an urgent need for people to be educated in ethical discernment, capable of seeing what is morally right,” he said in a speech at the Elysée.

At a second address on Friday, the 71-year-old head of the Catholic church insisted that new technologies must “remain at the service of the human person rather than becoming yet another instrument of domination and injustice” in remarks to a gathering at the Paris headquarters ⁠of the UN culture and education body, ⁠Unesco.

“Every science risks losing its proper meaning when pursued without ethics,” he said. “Certain artificial systems have even been given the name of our human faculty of thought: intelligence. At the same time, however, our ideas and relationships risk being impoverished by a process of dehumanisation.”

He added: “While intelligence is attributed to computational systems, we struggle to recognise the inalienable dignity of human persons whose lives are judged according to the criterion of efficiency and when deemed no longer productive, rejected and discarded.”

Leo also criticised world leaders who disrespect the ⁠rule of ⁠law, without naming individuals. “Instead of ​respecting ‌the law, ‌those in power invoke ‌it when it serves their interests and disregard it when it restrains them, treating even justice itself ‌as though it were a commodity to be ​bought and sold,” he said.
Leo, who became pope in 2025, ⁠has been critical of the direction ​of ​global leadership in ​recent months. He ​said ‌the world was “being ​ravaged ​by a handful of tyrants” last April.

blocks.caption: Pope Leo with the French president, Emmanuel Macron, and his wife, Brigitte Macron, at the Elysée. Photograph: Maurizio Brambatti/AP

blocks.text: The first official papal visit to France in 18 years comes as Emmanuel Macron’s decade in office draws to an end ahead of next spring’s French presidential election, for which the far-right, anti-immigration Marine Le Pen is polling high. Pope Francis did not make a full state visit to France during his 12-year pontificate and refused to join the inauguration of the rebuilt Notre Dame Cathedral in 2024.

After France passed legislation in June granting some adult patients the right to assisted dying, the pontiff said he was concerned by trends “that risk turning science and technology into profit-driven ventures promoting genetic manipulation, surrogacy, the trade in human organs or the possibility of arranging one’s own death.”
A key moment of the three-day visit will be a giant outdoor mass on Saturday, led by the pontiff at Place de la Concorde.

The pope, whose paternal grandmother was born in France, on Friday urged Paris to remain a “tireless champion of peace” worldwide. On Monday, he will deliver a speech on European peace in the eastern city of Metz as Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine continues into its fifth year.
Leo called on the world not to ⁠become indifferent to the pain caused by “the scourge of war”.
He told Macron and other French politicians: “I urge you '… never to grow resigned to the prospect of war or to ⁠consider it ‘inevitable’.”

Leo will also visit Lourdes, a pilgrimage site for Christians worldwide, where he will privately meet seven victims of clerical sex abuse. After some survivors’ groups suggested a larger number of survivors should have been canvassed, the Catholic church said the pontiff was seeking in-depth dialogue with individuals.

France’s Catholic bishops’ conference has agreed to provide compensation after a 2021 report estimated 330,000 children were sexually abused over 70 years by priests or other church-related figures in France. The report described a “systemic” cover-up by church officials.
In recent years, further accusations have emerged, including against workers at the elite Catholic boarding school, Bétharram, near Lourdes.

On his flight to Paris, Pope Leo told reporters they were welcome to cover him, as he responded to the Trump administration’s attempt to bar US media from the White House and affirmed the importance of journalists covering public figures.
Asked by a CNN reporter about Donald Trump’s attempt to bar CNN and other reporters, Leo said the media were welcome on his plane. “I am very happy that here, you are all welcome,” he said.

articles.title: RCMP watchdog postpones report from 3-year review on B.C. protest policing due to snap election
articles.summary: First Nations leaders and civil liberties advocates are concerned after the RCMP's federal review agency postponed release of a much-anticipated investigation into protest policing in British…

image.caption: On Jan. 7, 2019, RCMP enforced an injunction ordering people to stop preventing Coastal GasLink workers from accessing a road and bridge. (Chantelle Bellrichard/CBC)

blocks.text: Indigenous

First Nations leaders and civil liberties advocates are concerned after the RCMP's federal review agency postponed release of a much-anticipated investigation into protest policing in British Columbia due to the snap election call.
Report on Community-Industry Response Group 'should be released right away,' says regional chief

The Civilian Review and Complaints Commission (CRCC) said it wants to avoid any perception of interference in the election period and ensure its report on the Community-Industry Response Group (C-IRG), a specialized unit known for tactical operations on Wet'suwet'en territory and Fairy Creek, receives appropriate consideration.
But that's "an excuse," according to one First Nations leader who said the report will have wide-reaching implications and should be released when it's done, regardless of an election.
"Many people, especially those that are affected by this, are disappointed and I think there's no excuses," said Terry Teegee, regional chief of the B.C. Assembly of First Nations.
"It should be released right away considering that it may have implications on issues we're dealing with in the future."

The complaints commission intended to release on Wednesday the findings of a three-year probe into C-IRG, which was formed in 2017 to police protests against major resource extraction projects, namely the Trans Mountain pipeline expansion.
After B.C. NDP leader David Eby called an early election on Tuesday, the CRCC emailed CBC Indigenous explaining the decision to postpone.

"During an election period, the provincial government operates under caretaker conventions, which limit its ability to address or respond to matters that could be viewed as involving policy, administration, or future government decision-making," the email said.

"Publishing the report while the province is in caretaker mode would therefore make it difficult for the relevant provincial authorities to fully consider and respond to its findings and recommendations."
The review body delayed publication until a new government is sworn in and normal government operations have resumed, the email added.

The CRCC began the systemic investigation in 2023 after receiving more than 500 formal complaints about C-IRG's enforcement actions during the Wet'suwet'en-led resistance against the Coastal GasLink pipeline and the Fairy Creek anti-logging protests.

items: RCMP at Coastal GasLink pipeline blockade raid worried about weapons, booby traps
Injunctions justify RCMP spending near $50M on resource standoffs, B.C. Mountie says

blocks.text: Teegee said the findings should be treated with urgency given Prime Minister Mark Carney's focus on economic growth through pipelines, mines and other major infrastructure development.
"The West Coast oil pipeline or any other projects in the near future will be heavily scrutinized and perhaps this issue of protests will come up again," Teegee said.
"And then how does the RCMP react? Is this going to happen again?"
Wet'suwet'en Hereditary Chief Na'Moks (John Ridsdale) expressed identical concerns in an interview on Thursday.
"With this other delay, they're ignoring all the harms that have been committed," Na'Moks said.

"We're concerned here that they've been present at, like, pro-Palestinian encampments, UBC, and continued to expand their agenda. There's no doubt this will be increased given Carney's agenda and widespread opposition."
A spokesperson for the B.C. Civil Liberties Association said the delay seems to be a discretionary decision, not something that's required.

"A lot of people have been waiting for this report to be released, and it is a matter that is in the national interest as well as the interest of British Columbians," said BCCLA staff counsel Veronica Martisius.
Saying "justice delayed is justice denied," Martisius noted that release of the systemic investigation was already delayed for months because the CRCC's decision-maker position was vacant.

items: 'Significant delays' will impact completion of RCMP C-IRG probe, review agency says
RCMP has spent nearly $50M on policing pipeline, logging standoffs in B.C.

blocks.text: "I just don't think that police accountability is a partisan issue. That further delay will just damage the CRCC's credibility in terms of its ability to motivate police in this country to do better."

C-IRG has already faced numerous legal actions, including a proposed class-action lawsuit at Fairy Creek, a lawsuit from media outlet the Narwhal and photojournalist Amber Bracken, and a lawsuit from three Wet'suwet'en Nation members.

The RCMP formally apologized in 2025 for breaching reporter Jerome Turner's rights on Wet'suwet'en territory in 2020. A B.C. judge found officers' conduct during arrests on Wet'suwet'en territory in November 2021 involved racism and Charter breaches.
C-IRG was renamed the Critical Response Unit, or CRU-BC, and continues to operate, despite a coalition of lawyers, leaders, academics calling for a pause during the review, Na'Moks said.
He is skeptical about the potential for change because, while the CRCC makes findings and recommendations, it falls on the Mounties to implement them.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Brett Forester is a senior reporter with CBC Indigenous in Ottawa. He is a member of the Chippewas of Kettle and Stony Point First Nation in southern Ontario who previously worked as a journalist with the Aboriginal Peoples Television Network.

articles.title: No snap election before 2029, Andy Burnham says
articles.summary:
Prime minister quashes speculation that Labour’s revival in the polls could prompt early contest

•

blocks.text: Andy Burnham has said he will not call a general election before 2029, after days of speculation that Labour’s revival in the polls could tempt him to call an early contest.
The prime minister was repeatedly questioned on the prospect during a round of broadcast interviews to regional media on Friday.

He initially said he was “not particularly” tempted by the idea of an early election, but later became firmer, saying he would “knock that dead” and he was “not going to do that” because he was focused on getting on with the job.
Asked by ITV Calendar whether the next election would be in 2029, Burnham said: “Well, yes, that’s when the next election will be. All of this speculation on an early election, I can knock that dead.

“You know, people want me, new in office, to be getting on with the job of delivering on the things that we’ve discussed, rather than putting self-serving politics before that, which was what I would be doing if I call an election. I’m not going to do that.”

Talk of an early election had grown during the last week after polls showed Labour pulling into the lead with support in the low 20s, and the Conservatives and Reform neck-and-neck a few points behind them.

Westminster sources said Downing Street advisers and MPs had been discussing the merits of an early poll but that even though the right was split, Labour would be at risk of losing its majority and having to form a coalition.

The Guardian revealed on Friday that Ravinder Athwal, the economist who wrote Labour’s 2024 manifesto, was taking on a senior role as an adviser to John Healey, the chancellor, to strengthen his team before the budget. This fuelled further speculation that the party’s preparations for a campaign were gathering pace.
Athwal, a Cambridge economics graduate, devised Keir Starmer’s five “missions”, which were meant to shape Labour’s approach to government.
Healey poached Athwal to be his senior special adviser from the business advisory group Flint Global, previously run by Burnham’s chief of staff, James Purnell, a Blair-era cabinet minister.
All the parties had begun increasing their preparations for a potential campaign since Burnham replaced Starmer in the summer, in case he decided to take advantage of the bounce in his popularity.

However, the prime minister has repeatedly ruled it out, both before and after taking office. In his regional interviews, he stressed his attention was on the party’s autumn conference, saying a big focus of his speech would be on setting out more details of a new model for the water industry that increases public control.

He told BBC South: “As we go into the Labour conference, we will set out more thinking about the change that we need to see in the running of water across the country. But it is clear to me that what we’ve had in the last 30 years is nowhere near good enough and is actually letting the public pay.”
Leading up to the conference in Liverpool, Labour members have been cheered by Burnham’s takeover, which has led to a modest recovery in the party’s popularity.

An MRP poll of more than 8,000 voters reported by the Guardian this week showed a significant shift of left-leaning voters towards Burnham’s Labour. This encouraged those in the party who have been thinking of gambling on an early election while Reform’s ratings are ebbing and while leftwing parties such as the Greens appear to be losing momentum.

Twice as many voters have returned to Labour from the left as from the right since April. The previously unreleased research, including a seat-by-seat MRP model, was conducted by Survation and the progressive activist site 38 Degrees in Burnham’s first month as prime minister.
It also showed progressive voters could push Reform UK into fourth place and put Labour within touching distance of a majority if tactical voting was widespread.
Burnham is beginning to attract a significant number of left-leaning voters back to Labour, motivated by a desire to stop Nigel Farage, the results suggest.

articles.title: Leviste in France taking care of mom Loren
articles.summary: Batangas 1st District Rep. Leandro Leviste is in France taking care of his mother, Sen. Loren Legarda, who is undergoing treatment for a lung and autoimmune condition.

blocks.text: September 26, 2026 | 12:00am
MANILA, Philippines — Batangas 1st District Rep. Leandro Leviste is in France taking care of his mother, Sen. Loren Legarda, who is undergoing treatment for a lung and autoimmune condition.

“She is with Leandro, who is the one assisting her with her medical needs in the family. As you know, Leandro is her main family now, and that’s what he is doing now,” Legarda’s spokesperson Tony La Viña told reporters during the Pandesal Forum in Quezon City.
La Viña did not give further details about the status of Legarda’s health, noting that the Senate knows about her condition.
“It’s not just now. It’s been like this for a long time, but it’s aggravated when there’s stress, when there’s tension,” he said.
As the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte comes to a close in November, La Viña is not ruling out that Legarda will be back as she took her oath as senator-judge.
La Viña noted that Leviste will also return to the country once his mother gets better: “After all, he’s just there with his mother. What reason would there be (not to come home)?”
The mother and son are facing probes over their solar franchises.

articles.title: China blocks Ayungin resupply mission anew
articles.summary: The military’s rotation and resupply (RORE) mission to the West Philippine Sea (WPS) did not reach its destination after 15 Chinese vessels shadowed it 60 nautical miles from Ayungin Shoal…

blocks.text: September 26, 2026 | 12:00am

A People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) warship, five Chinese maritime militia ships and nine China Coast Guard (CCG) vessels ganged up on civilian supply boat M/V Lapu-Lapu, despite being escorted by three ships from the Philippine Navy and Philippine Coast Guard.
Armed Forces of the Philippines

MANILA, Philippines — The military’s rotation and resupply (RORE) mission to the West Philippine Sea (WPS) did not reach its destination after 15 Chinese vessels shadowed it 60 nautical miles from Ayungin Shoal Thursday night.
PCG spokesman for the WPS Rear Admiral Jay Tarriela said the mission was discontinued at around 11:08 p.m. due to safety concerns.
“The PLA Navy warship issued a radio challenge warning that it would take ‘compulsory measures’ against the resupply mission,” Tarriela said.
The PCG noted that the CCG vessels shadowing M/V Lapu-Lapu made a maneuver of nearly 1,000 yards, which could have led to a collision.
“Our Coast Guard vessel, BRP Malabrigo, which was deployed to provide security assistance, was also shadowed by CCG vessels,” Tarriela said.
M/V Lapu-Lapu was supposed to deliver essential supplies and personnel to the BRP Sierra Madre stationed in Ayungin Shoal.
Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) spokesman for the WPS retired rear admiral Roy Vincent Trinidad, said the incident happened between 8:35 p.m. to 11 p.m. Thursday.

“They did not technically block (our ships) but we were being monitored, driven away, and they were inching closer and closer. From miles until yards, thousands of yards, hundreds of yards – so to avoid escalation, it was the judgment call of the ground commander, the unified commander (to abort),” Trinidad explained.

“These actions are irresponsible, are reckless and are inconsistent with applicable provisions of COLREGs (Convention on the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea) and UNCLOS (United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea), as well as the Philippines’ rights affirmed by the 2016 Arbitral Award,” the AFP said.
Trinidad said it is now up to the unified commander on how to carry out a new RORE mission to Ayungin Shoal based on contingency plans in place.
According to him, the AFP does not consider China’s radio messages as radio challenges because the area in question belongs to the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone.
In a separate statement, the National Task Force for the West Philippine Sea denounced China’s interference of a lawful Philippine RORE mission.

“CCG and PLA Navy vessels hindered a routine mission to deliver essential supplies to, and rotate the personnel stationed aboard BRP Sierra Madre (LS57). In doing so, they put Filipino personnel at risk and obstructed a legitimate humanitarian and sustainment operation.”
Philippines committed to protect maritime infrastructure
Meanwhile, the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) gave assurance on the country’s commitment to working with the United Nations in protecting critical maritime infrastructure.

Speaking on the sidelines of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly High-Level Week Ministerial Meeting in New York, DFA Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro said that “as an archipelagic nation situated at the crossroads of the Indo-Pacific, the Philippines lives the maritime reality every single day.”
“Our presence here today reflects a shared resolve: to ensure that our oceans remain spaces of cooperation, connection, and peace, rather than arenas of vulnerability,” she noted.

articles.title: SWS: 52 percent of Pinoys feel helpless vs corruption
articles.summary: A majority of Filipinos feel helpless about corruption in the government, a recent survey by the Social Weather Stations (SWS) showed.

blocks.text: September 26, 2026 | 12:00am
Commuters disembark at LRT-1 Central Terminal Station in Manila on April 16, 2026, the temporary last stop for trains from Fernando Poe Jr. Station following limited operations.
The STAR / Ryan Baldemor
MANILA, Philippines — A majority of Filipinos feel helpless about corruption in the government, a recent survey by the Social Weather Stations (SWS) showed.
The survey, conducted from June 20 to 29, found 52 percent agreeing with the statement: “a person like me cannot do anything to reduce corruption in the government.”
Thirty-percent disagreed with the statement while 17 percent were undecided.
SWS said the net score, obtained by subtracting those who disagreed from those who agreed with the statement, remained at a “worse-on-record” -22.
It hardly moved from -23 obtained in a similar survey in March (51 percent agree, 29 percent disagree).

Across areas, respondents who felt helpless about corruption were highest among those in Metro Manila at 64 percent, followed by those in the rest of Luzon at 55 percent, Mindanao at 47 percent and Visayas at 42 percent.

Before this year, the last time a similar survey asked the same question was in December 2009, when 41 percent said they could not do anything to reduce corruption. Another 41 percent disagreed with the statement.

A 2012 survey, meanwhile, found that 60 percent of the respondents agreed to the statement: “it is too difficult for someone like me to fight corruption in the government.” Nineteen percent disagreed with the statement, while 20 percent were undecided.
The latest poll had 1,200 respondents and a margin of error of plus/minus three percent.

articles.title: DOTr lifts suspension of PUV fare hike
articles.summary: The approved fare hike for public utility vehicles will finally be implemented after the Department of Transportation (DOTr) yesterday lifted its earlier suspension.

blocks.text: September 26, 2026 | 12:00am
Motorists crawl through heavy traffic along EDSA–Taft Avenue in Pasay City on January 4, 2026 as vehicles pass through sections reopened following the ongoing EDSA rehabilitation project.
Ryan Baldemor / The Philippine STAR
MANILA, Philippines — The approved fare hike for public utility vehicles will finally be implemented after the Department of Transportation (DOTr) yesterday lifted its earlier suspension.

Transportation Secretary Giovanni Lopez confirmed to The STAR the issuance of a memorandum to the Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) lifting the suspension on fare adjustments.
The DOTr directed the LTFRB to ensure that operators and drivers post the new fare matrices inside their vehicles before charging the adjusted fares.
Under the fare hike approved in March, an increase of P1 for traditional jeepneys raises the minimum fare to P14. For modern jeepneys, a P2 increase brings the minimum fare to P17.

For ordinary Metro Manila/ city buses, P2 increase, from P13 to P15; for air-conditioned Metro Manila/city buses, P3 increase, from P15 to P18; for ordinary provincial buses, P1 increase, from P11 to P12; and for air-conditioned provincial buses, P2.45 increase per succeeding kilometer.
For airport taxis, a P40 increase in flag-down rate for the first 500 meters raises it to P115.
Likewise, there will be a 20 percent increase in TNVS’ base fare, depending on vehicle type and a 15 percent hike in fares for P2P buses.

articles.title: Mark Villar to remain with minority – Cayetano
articles.summary: Sen. Mark Villar will remain with the minority bloc despite his recent vote to alter the conviction threshold denominator in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, Minority Leader Alan…

blocks.text: September 26, 2026 | 12:00am
Sen. Mark Villar appears during the convening of the impeachment court at the Senate, May 18, 2026.
Mark Villar via Facebook

MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Mark Villar will remain with the minority bloc despite his recent vote to alter the conviction threshold denominator in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano said yesterday.
Clarifying the dynamics within the chamber, Cayetano emphasized that political alignments do not dictate how senator-judges vote in the ongoing trial.
Villar recently broke ranks with his minority colleagues who decided to sit out Wednesday’s vote on the threshold.

“He’s staying with the minority,” Cayetano told reporters. “There is no minority-minority when it comes to the impeachment court. So, if there will be consultations, it would be more of gauging each other, rather than wondering how we will vote as one.”
Cayetano noted that while senators frequently share meals, discuss legislation and consult each other on legal nuances, they maintain their independence as judges.
Despite Villar’s differing vote, Cayetano gave assurance that the bloc remains unified and operational.
However, he lamented the ongoing absence of several members due to legal and medical issues.

“(The minority is) working. There is no animosity here in the minority. Of course, we long for the 11 to be complete, but then again, four of our colleagues are facing different challenges,” Cayetano said.

articles.title: Gatchalian: Without TRO, no stopping impeachment trial
articles.summary: Unless restrained by the Supreme Court (SC), there is no stopping the Senate from proceeding with the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte next week.

blocks.text: September 26, 2026 | 12:00am
Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian looks on during the start of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte at the Senate in Pasay, Metro Manila on July 6, 2026.
AFP / Jam Sta Rosa
MANILA, Philippines — Unless restrained by the Supreme Court (SC), there is no stopping the Senate from proceeding with the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte next week.

Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said the chamber would fulfill its constitutional mandate to try and decide the case, regardless of pending petitions seeking to nullify the proceedings or a potential boycott by the defense panel.

He issued the statement amid a petition for a restraining order filed with the SC by former executive secretary Vic Rodriguez, and a petition for a status quo ante order on the voting numbers to convict, which lawyer Ernesto Francisco Jr. filed yesterday.
Asked about the possibility of Duterte’s defense team skipping the trial, Gatchalian maintained that the Senate’s work continues.
He also affirmed that the Senate would strictly follow the new ruling on the conviction threshold denominator, stating that “the court made that decision so we will follow it.”

Impeachment court spokesman Reginald Tongol said the trial would proceed as scheduled on Monday – from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. – despite Malacañang’s declaration of a half-day work suspension for the 34th National Family Week.
Duterte was mum over the impeachment court’s ruling on allowing a lower number of votes to convict her.
“I’ll just leave it to the spokesperson of the defense team,” Duterte said.
She said that there is still no decision for her to attend the impeachment trial as the Senate impeachment court has yet to issue a subpoena.
“Impeachment is a legal process and the presence of my lawyers there is my appearance and participation,” she said. — Daphne Galvez, Helen Flores, Bella Cariaso

articles.title: OVP defends relief operations flagged by COA
articles.summary: The Office of the Vice President (OVP) yesterday defended its relief operation discrepancies after the Commission on Audit (COA) flagged the agency over inconsistencies, deviations from orders and…

blocks.text: September 26, 2026 | 12:00am
The photo of the Commission on Audit's office in Quezon CIty taken on August 17, 2021.
The STAR / Michael Varcas

MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the Vice President (OVP) yesterday defended its relief operation discrepancies after the Commission on Audit (COA) flagged the agency over inconsistencies, deviations from orders and missing or incomplete documents in relation to its P168 million worth of activities in 2025.

“The Office of the Vice President (OVP) clarifies that the matter cited in the Disaster Risk Reduction Management Funds Audit Report pertains to deficiencies in certain pre-operation documentary requirements set by the OVP itself as part of its internal procedures, and not requirements imposed by any law or Commission on Audit regulation,” it said.

In a 273-page report on the 2025 Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Fund, the COA said it found discrepancies in the situation reports prepared by the OVP and the validation prepared by local government units for relief operations involving P19.67 million worth of welfare goods.
Discrepancies were found in the reported number of affected families while some local government units did not indicate a beneficiary count.

“The discrepancies arose from changes in circumstances and field conditions that became apparent as the operations were carried out. No funds were lost and all funds are accounted for,” the OVP added.

The OVP maintained that the relief operations were actually carried out, and the beneficiaries were recorded and validated based on the available supporting documents and field records submitted to the COA Audit Team.

articles.title: VP Sara-Robin ahead of Leni-Bam in hypothetical matchup
articles.summary: A new survey by the OCTA Research group showed that more Filipinos prefer the hypothetical tandem of Vice President Sara Duterte and Sen. Robin Padilla, than Naga City Mayor Leni Robredo and Sen. Bam…

blocks.text: September 26, 2026 | 12:00am
Vice President Sara Duterte visits quake victims in Davao Occidental, as seen in photos posted June 26, 2026.
Duterte office

MANILA, Philippines — A new survey by the OCTA Research group showed that more Filipinos prefer the hypothetical tandem of Vice President Sara Duterte and Sen. Robin Padilla, than Naga City Mayor Leni Robredo and Sen. Bam Aquino, in the upcoming 2028 national elections.

The survey, conducted from July 4 to 11, found that 48 percent of the respondents would vote for Duterte and Padilla if they run against Robredo and Aquino for president and vice president, respectively.
Thirty-six percent said they would vote for the Robredo-Aquino tandem, while 16 percent were undecided.
Although the Duterte-Padilla tandem is ahead by 12 points, OCTA said this is the “narrowest gap recorded between the two tandems to date.”

“In previous commissioned surveys conducted in 2025, the gap between the tandem of VP Sara Duterte–Sen. Robin Padilla and the tandem of VP Leni Robredo-Sen. Bam Aquino had ranged from approximately 20 to 25 points, indicating a narrowing trend heading into 2028,” the polling firm said.
Only Duterte had declared her intention to run for a national post in 2028.
Padilla, who was frontrunner in the 2022 Senate race, already said he is not inclined to run as Duterte’s vice president.
Robredo said she prefers to run for a second term as Naga mayor, while Aquino – who ranked second in 2025 – already ruled out running for vice president in 2028.
The OCTA poll had 1,200 respondents and a margin of error of plus/minus three percent.

articles.title: Senate flags over 7,000 projects due to data anomalies
articles.summary: Questioning the lapsed legal mandate of acting Public Works Secretary Vince Dizon, the Senate flagged 7,107 Department of Public Works and Highways infrastructure projects worth P251 billion for data…

blocks.text: September 26, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — Questioning the lapsed legal mandate of acting Public Works Secretary Vince Dizon, the Senate flagged 7,107 Department of Public Works and Highways infrastructure projects worth P251 billion for data anomalies yesterday.

During the DPWH budget deliberations, Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said the projects required rigorous data cleanup by regional and district engineers before the Senate could finalize its committee report.
He warned that the DPWH central office could be overwhelmed if local engineers passed on messy or incomplete data involving nearly 12,000 projects overall.

“Our district engineers and regional directors should be the ones to clean up your data because of the sheer number of projects. There are almost 12,000 projects, and if they all reach the central office, it will be very difficult for them to clean up,” Gatchalian said. “Hopefully, I’m assuming this is not intentional. I hope.”

Gatchalian said his office identified eight red flags, including duplicated projects, misplaced or missing station numbers, missing coordinates, lump-sum appropriations, overlapping projects, unspecified work scope and conflicting types of work.
He also flagged projects that were already funded in 2026 but reappeared in the proposed 2027 budget.
Expired mandate
Sen. Imee Marcos, meanwhile, questioned Dizon over his lapsed legal mandate to lead the DPWH, noting that Dizon was appointed in an acting capacity in September last year.
Citing the Administrative Code of 1987, she said temporary designations cannot exceed one year.
“Today is what, Sept. 25, 2026? Overdue na po kayo ng ilang araw, 24 days. What is the present status, therefore, of your appointment?” Marcos told Dizon yesterday.
Dizon said he was informed by his staff that the Office of the President considers his appointment as “continuing.”
Marcos rejected the “holdover” justification, arguing that the principle cannot override an explicit prohibition in the law.
Dizon said he would gladly step down if he were legally required to do so.
“To be quite frank, it would be very welcome if what you’re saying is that I am no longer the DPWH secretary. I will be more than happy to accept that,” he said.
Marcos ended the exchange by demanding a formal legal explanation from the DPWH regarding Dizon’s exact status.
The House of Representatives, for its part, concluded plenary deliberations on the proposed P643.95-billion DPWH budget for 2027, with stricter safeguards for infrastructure projects.
As part of its reforms to curb corruption, Dizon said more than 11,000 infrastructure projects would be posted on a transparency portal for public review and scrutiny.
Romualdez to take witness stand

In a related development on the flood control scandal, former Speaker Martin Romualdez will “most likely” take the witness stand to defend himself in the P7.4 billion plunder case against him over his alleged involvement in the controversial kickback scheme from flood control projects, according to his lawyer.
“He wants his day to defend himself in court, and he will most likely testify,” lawyer Ade Fajardo said.
He said the alleged bagmen of co-defendant Zaldy Co could also be called to testify. — Emmanuel Tupas, Daphne Galvez

articles.title: Typhoons may bring unprecedented rainfall – UP study
articles.summary: Typhoons could bring unprecedented rainfall as the atmosphere warms, according to a 2026 study by experts from the University of the Philippines.

blocks.text: September 26, 2026 | 12:00am
A meteorologist of the Manila City Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Department monitors Tropical Storm Queenie, which has entered the Philippine area of responsibility.
Edd Gumban
MANILA, Philippines — Typhoons could bring unprecedented rainfall as the atmosphere warms, according to a 2026 study by experts from the University of the Philippines.

Researchers from the UP Institute of Environmental Science and Meteorology Climate and High Impact Weather Laboratory, led by Rafaela Jane Delfino, said the atmosphere can hold roughly seven percent more water vapor for every degree Celsius of warming, citing the Clausius-Clapeyron relationship.
The scientists said typhoons such as Super Typhoon Yolanda are highly efficient at drawing moisture and converting it into precipitation.
Additional moisture from warming was the dominant driver for tropical cyclones Yolanda, Pablo and Ompong, while storm dynamics varied from cyclone to cyclone.
“With the findings of our paper, it becomes very important to know in advance where a typhoon will pass, where it will make landfall, and where it will go afterward,” Delfino said.
Urging a shift in how the country prepares for disasters, researchers she said disasters should not be understood or prepared for as isolated events.
Queenie to intensify
Meanwhile, Tropical Storm Queenie is expected to intensify into a typhoon over the weekend, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration said yesterday.
PAGASA weather specialist John Manalo said Queenie (Surigae) may develop into a typhoon near the boundary of the Philippine area of responsibility.
As of 4 p.m. yesterday, Queenie was 755 kilometers east of Basco, Batanes, packing winds of 85 km per hour and gusts of up to 105 kph while moving west-northwest at 20 kph.

The intertropical convergence zone will bring cloudy skies with scattered rains and thunderstorms over Negros Island Region, Central Visayas, Zamboanga Peninsula, Northern Mindanao, Caraga, Davao Oriental and Basilan. — Josiah Antonio

articles.title: Trump faces tough choices as Iran dangles deal to reopen Hormuz before US midterms
articles.summary:
Iran’s seven-day timetable would restart nuclear talks, but will the US be willing to deliver on terms that include reining in Israel in Lebanon?

Iran’s seven-day timetable to reopen…

blocks.text: Iran’s seven-day timetable to reopen the strait of Hormuz and start talks on its nuclear programme has been pitched as a deal that could rapidly extricate Donald Trump from a political crisis but requires the US president to make difficult concessions.

In the five days left before the proposed reopening of the strait, which is expected to relieve pressure on global energy markets, Trump would need to lift Iranian asset freezes, permit Iran to export its oil and, probably most difficult of all, order Benjamin Netanyahu to end Israel’s attacks on Hezbollah in Lebanon, thus achieving the “ceasefire on all fronts”.

Iranian diplomats in New York said they thought a three-hour meeting earlier this week with the US envoy Steve Witkoff in which they laid out the seven-day plan was productive, but were doubtful the US would deliver.
Iran nevertheless feels it has done the diplomatic spadework, taking the proposal to China for endorsement and ensuring that Oman, located on the south side of the strait, was also on board.

The foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, explained that the idea was to take the elements of the Iran-US memorandum of understanding that Trump signed in June and repackage and accelerate the process since, as they understood it, Trump had come to hate the MoU.

“The conditions we have asked the US to meet is nothing new, nothing more than what was already in the Islamabad agreement, which was signed by the US president,” Araghchi said. But what is new is the speed.

blocks.caption: Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, says the new deal contains the elements of June’s memorandum of understanding. Photograph: Alexi J Rosenfeld/Getty Images

blocks.text: In the first four to five days under this timetable, the US will have to lift the naval blockade on Iran’s oil ports, restore the waiver lifting sanctions on Iran’s oil exports, end the war on all fronts and permit the release of some of Iran’s frozen assets.

On the sixth day, the strait of Hormuz would be reopened by Iran with ships using a new route designated by Oman and Iran. And on the next day, negotiations will start on the future of Iran’s civil nuclear programme, including a protocol to allow UN nuclear inspectors back in to look at Iran’s damaged sites and the Iranian stockpile of highly enriched uranium. This accelerates the point at which nuclear talks would begin from 60 days in the June agreement to seven.

Those talks could, of course, then take a long time, but from Trump’s perspective, the strait of Hormuz would be reopened before the midterm elections, a point in the political calendar that the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, says has never been a factor in Iranian thinking. Trump had claimed Iran was waiting until after the vote to offer a deal.
Iran, Araghchi argued at a largely off-the-record briefing with reporters – at which Pezeshkian was also present – has every reason not to negotiate with the US.

In particular, he admitted to being sceptical that Witkoff could deliver. He recounted how he had twice held talks with Trump’s special envoy, with Witkoff saying the talks had been “productive and good”, only for Iran to be bombed by the US the next day. Other Iranian diplomats say Trump’s willingness to rein in Netanyahu in Lebanon remains key. If he were to do that, a deal would be feasible.

It is a difficult deal for Trump to swallow since the strait would reopen largely on Iran’s terms, with the new route predominantly going through Iranian waters. Saudi Arabia is also concerned that the route deal is bilateral between Iran and Oman, and not with the Gulf states as joint signatories.

blocks.caption: Is Trump prepared to go back to war with Iran after the midterm elections? Photograph: Mike Segar/Reuters

blocks.text: Trump says he has a choice to make between the annihilation of Iran and engagement – an engagement that he says, with typical hyperbole, could make Iran one of the great countries of the world. In reality, the judgement he has to make is more prosaic. Is he prepared to go back to war with Iran, after the midterms and, if not, does he believe the US can squeeze the Iranian economy so hard that the leadership will succumb.

Pezeshkian – who handed all questions about the talks to Araghchi, who was sitting to his right – admitted Iranians wanted the war to end and did not deny the economic pressure, but said the public had withstood sanctions for 45 years.

He also insisted Iran’s decision-making machinery was functioning. The reclusive supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei was completely healthy, he claimed – a testimony based on spending seven hours in his presence. He did not explain what, apart from security, led Khamenei to not even issue a voice recording, photograph, let alone a video, as proof of life.

articles.title: Students strike across Germany in protest against military service
articles.summary: A law establishing voluntary military service came into effect in January, but protest organisers fear compulsory service could follow.

blocks.text: School strikes are taking place across Germany to protest against the possible reintroduction of compulsory military service.

One of the organisers of the strike, Bela Breitner, from School Strike Against Compulsory Military Service said the federal government was "serious about gradually reintroducing compulsory military service".
At one protest in Hamburg, demonstrators waved flags and held up banners emblazoned with the words "We won't take part in your wars".
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has made boosting Germany's military a priority following Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
A new law introducing voluntary military service came into force in January, with the aim of recruiting volunteers to increase the number of soldiers.
However, if the security situation worsens or if too few volunteers come forward, a form of compulsory military service could be considered by Germany's Parliament, the Bundestag.
Under the law, all 18-year-olds in Germany are being sent a questionnaire asking if they are interested and willing to join the armed forces.
One protester, 16-year-old Elias Bernhard, from Hamburg, said that the responses to the questionnaires "show that young people do not want to join the Bundeswehr [Germany's army]".
"That is why I am out on the streets today. That is why we are serious about striking until compulsory military service is off the table. We will carry on."
The questionnaire is mandatory for men and voluntary for women. All 18-year-old men will have to take a medical exam to assess their fitness for possible military service.

The organisers of the protests, say the trigger came after some 18-year-olds in the northern German towns of Kiel and Flensburg, were sent official invitations for medical exams, even though they expressed no interest in joining the army on their registration forms.
The group says over a hundred demonstrations are planned across Germany, including in Kiel, Hamburg, Berlin and Frankfurt.

A spokesperson for the Defence Ministry told the BBC that under the law, the obligation to undergo a medical examination applies "to all men liable for military service who were born after 31 December 2007".

This also applies to people who have stated that they have no interest in compulsory military service. The spokesperson said that since July around 1,000 18-year-old men, who showed no interest in the army, have had the medical exam.
During the Cold War, Germany, like many other European countries, had a large army. But it reduced its armed forces during the 1990s after the fall of the Iron Curtain.
Germany's former Chancellor, Angela Merkel, ended compulsory military service in 2011.
But now, in the face of perceived threats from Russia and heavy pressure from Germany's traditional ally, the US, Merz has vowed to transform the Bundeswehr into Europe's strongest conventional army.

The Bundeswehr currently has around 186,700 troops. By the early 2030s, Germany wants to raise the number to 260,000, supplemented by around 200,000 reservists, in order to meet new Nato force targets and strengthen Germany's defences.

MANILA, Philippines – In her first one-on-one interview since receiving an absolute pardon, former overseas Filipino worker Mary Jane Veloso sits down with Rappler’s Jairo Bolledo on Friday, September 25, to discuss her newly attained freedom.

Veloso was granted an absolute pardon by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Thursday, September 24, paving the way for her freedom after 16 years of detention. Fourteen of those years were spent in an Indonesian prison, and nearly two at the Correctional Institution for Women (CIW) in Mandaluyong City.
Veloso was issued a discharge certificate from the CIW on Friday, the same day the pardon was made public.

articles.title: Senior Kazakh officials detained after 14 service members swept out to sea
articles.summary: Seventeen service members were swept out to the Caspian Sea during military exercises.

blocks.text: Five senior military officials have been detained in Kazakhstan following the death of 14 service members who were taking part in military exercises.

Those who died were among a total of 17 who were swept into the Caspian Sea as they were disembarking from a boat on Thursday. Officials say the incident occurred "during a combat training mission due to a sharp deterioration in meteorological conditions and increasing winds".
Three were rescued.

Those detained include the chief of staff and first deputy commander of Kazakhstan's Naval Forces, two military unit commanders, and the commanders of a marine company and a boat. They are suspected of criminal negligence.
An interior ministry committee has been set up to investigate the incident, which occurred some 43km (27 miles) from the city of Aktau in south-western Kazakstan.
Deputy Interior Minister Sanzhar Adilov said a pretrial investigation into the deaths was being conducted.

The investigation was looking into the decisions made during the organisation and execution of the military training exercise, whether safety requirements had been observed, and weather conditions had been taken into account - in addition to technical specifications of the boat.
More than 500 military personnel, warships and coastal units were participating in the Caspian Defense 2026 military exercise, according to the Kazakh ministry of defence.

articles.title: Pakistan's Sharif rails against India, praises Trump at UNGA
articles.summary: Pakistan's prime minister blamed India for last year's clashes, and credited the US president with preventing "all-out war" between two nuclear powers. Albania's PM told the UN delegates an anecdote…
articles.byline: Wesley Dockery, Mark Hallam, Felix Tamsut, Jon Shelton

image.caption: Sharif portrayed his country as a would-be peacemaker in Iran and branded India the aggressor in South Asia Image: Yuki Iwamura/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: September 25, 2026
Sharif blames India for 2025 clashes, calls for 'just and fair' Kashmir resolution

blocks.caption: Sharif elicited shakes of the head from India with his commentsImage: Yuki Iwamura/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also took aim at India in his speech as he discussed the limited military clashes between the uneasy neighbors last year.

"A year ago, Pakistan faced external aggression from India under a false pretext," the prime minister alleged. "Pakistan exercised its inherent right of self-defense under Article 51 of the United Nations charter."

He praised the country's military saying, "They silenced the enemy, repulsed its attack, and taught it a lesson it shall never ever forget," as the UN's TV feed cut to an Indian observer in the assembly shaking his head as he listened.

Pakistan considers Indian missile strikes on May 7 to be the start of the low-level conflict, that ran for less than a week, while India contends that the strikes were retalliation for an attack in Indian-administered Jammu and Kashmir in late April. New Delhi had accused Pakistan of supporting cross-border terrorism, which Islambad denied.

Sharif praised US President Donald Trump's "resolute and visionary leadership," crediting it with saving "hundreds of millions of lives in South Asia" by intervening and helping to broker a truce "when two nuclear neighbors stood at the brink of all-out war."
Sharif asked "who knows the extent of devastation that could have taken place" without Trump's "clarity of thought and action" at a critical moment.
He said it was necessary to ensure that South Asia "never reaches this precipice again," and said that doing so would require "a just and fair resolution of the Kashmir dispute."

He said Kashmiri people had been waiting eight decades for the UN to "fulfill its solemn commitment of a free and impartial plebiscite under its auspices." He also criticized recent "attempts to alter the legal status of Jammu and Kashmir through demographic reengineering and other illegal measures."
He also criticized India for its decision to hold a treat on the Indus River System in abeyance, saying this move had "no legal basis whatsoever."

articles.title: OpenAI hack on Australian government reveals anxiety at heart of global artificial intelligence dilemma
articles.summary:
As the UN warns traditional safeguards are ‘unravelling’, Donald Trump says he will encourage, not restrain, the AI race

When the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, sat down for an…

blocks.text: When the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, sat down for an interview in the heart of Silicon Valley at the weekend he had known for two days that his was the first government known to have been attacked by a rogue AI agent.
He didn’t reveal the attack then, but he sounded a warning about the march of AI: “the risk is that AI develops in a way in which humans are no longer in control of what AI is producing.”
But Albanese noted, too, that two countries – the US and China – would dominate the world’s response to the new technology.
“The truth is they’re the big two giants here, and so we want to see cooperation,” Albanese said.
“The US is essentially ahead of China when it comes to the race that is on for the development of this new technology. But it is in the world’s interests that there be engagement.”

Days later, Albanese used the global attention of the United Nations general assembly meeting in New York to reveal that Australia’s government healthcare system, Medicare, had been attacked by an OpenAI agent in June, but that it was three months before his government was told.
Again he warned of “the potential risks of allowing frontier AI to develop too fast without guardrails”.

China’s president, Xi Jinping, skipped the general assembly in favour of a bilateral meeting with the US president, where he emphasised the responsibility to manage AI “for good, and ensure that the development of AI is always under human control and serves the wellbeing of the people”.

But the president of the United States – the nation which is the global leader in artificial intelligence – used his general assembly address to insist he would only encourage, not restrain, the AI race.
Alarms sounding
To little fanfare earlier in the week, the UN’s independent international scientific panel on AI warned a threshold had already been crossed.

There was, the panel, said: “no assurance that humans can reliably keep AI agents under control today, particularly as they become more capable, harder to monitor and better at finding loopholes or hiding their activity”.
The Australian government had known the reality of this for more than a week. OpenAI had known it more than a month.
Two days after the panel’s statement, the Australian prime minister belatedly revealed an OpenAI agent had hacked medical data held by Australia’s universal health care provider, Medicare.
No patient data had been accessed, but the agent had gained unauthorised access to “non-public files”.

OpenAI’s agent hacked the government sites in June of this year. OpenAI discovered its agent had gone rogue in August. It did not tell the Australian government until 10 September, and then only with a solitary email to a generic public email address not checked until the next day. The prime minister was informed on 18 September.
It was another week before the Australian people were told.

Australia has promised, if it is possible, to lay criminal charges, though this is complicated by the fact that OpenAI claims the hack was committed by an AI agent – apparently acting beyond its instructions (euphemised by OpenAI as “misaligned behaviour”) – not a person.

The hack on Australia’s Medicare statistics reporting service portal, as well as three other government sites, follows the Hugging Face incident in July, in which autonomous AI agents developed by OpenAI broke out of their isolated testing environments, coordinated themselves into a “swarm” and launched a cyber-attack on competitor AI platform Hugging Face.

10.45am Deputy PM Richard Marles and Gallagher address Australian media.
The UN panel, investigating that attack, warned “the traditional method of safeguarding is unravelling” as AI agents act autonomously to breach protections.

“The default interpretation and immediate lesson is that basic cybersecurity practices were overlooked, and safeguards are not advancing at the pace of capabilities. The more insidious and grave concern is that current training methods can lead agents to adopt goals of their own, knowingly violate safety instructions, and conceal their actions.”
Twenty countries (including Australia) and the EU this week signed a statement arguing the rapid development of frontier AI models posed serious risks to safety and security if not properly managed.
“AI must remain under human direction, oversight and control. It must be developed and used in line with international law.”
Too soon?
Even those running AI companies have warned the technology is developing too rapidly for humans to control.

Appearing before the UN security council this week, OpenAI’s chief executive, Sam Altman, warned: “some of the things people working to build AI have said are so dystopian that they sound like the plot of bad science fiction movies”.
“As AI systems become more capable and more autonomous, they can move faster than our institutions … or make decisions that people no longer understand or control.”
But there are at least two – very loud – voices in opposition to any external regulation of the AI industry.

blocks.caption: Elon Musk has said AI would probably be beyond human control within a decade, and that humanity should ‘enjoy the ride’. Photograph: Susan Walsh/AP

blocks.text: Elon Musk, who co-founded OpenAI with Altman before falling out with him, said in a recent interview the “smart move” would be to have the “leading AI companies at least just meet or have some sort of call once every few weeks and just discuss any safety and security issues”.
Musk said AI would probably be beyond the control of humans within a decade, and that humanity should “enjoy the ride”.

“I still think there’s risk associated with AI and robots. It’s not zero … my sort of philosophical conclusion is to look on the bright side. I can’t see any way to really stop this incredible momentum of AI and robots.
“If there was a stop button, we probably shouldn’t press it, because the most likely outcome is incredible abundance for all.”
Donald Trump used his speech to the UN general assembly to attempt to rebrand AI, and insist it should never be reined in.
“The United States also totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control for the artificial intelligence being spoken of so much now,” the US president said.
Trump wants to re-label artificial intelligence “superintelligence”.
“I’m not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution.
“We’re going to encourage it, not rein it in.”
Trump said the US was “leading China by a lot” in AI, and would continue to do so “safely and responsibly”.
“Whoever wins superintelligence, wins.”

articles.title: Mary Jane Veloso freed from prison hours after Marcos announced pardon
articles.summary: Former OFW Mary Jane Veloso has been freed from the Correctional Institution for Women in Mandaluyong hours after President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. announced that he had signed her absolute…

blocks.text: Published September 25, 2026 11:12pm

Former OFW Mary Jane Veloso has been freed from the Correctional Institution for Women in Mandaluyong hours after President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. announced that he had signed her absolute pardon.
According to Chino Gaston’s report on “Saksi,” the Bureau of Corrections received at 5 p.m. from the Department of Justice the order for Veloso’s release. It was processed immediately.
A beaming Veloso faced the media with BuCor chief Gregorio Catapang Jr., during which she thanked Marcos.
“Ito na po ‘yung araw na pinakahihintay ko,” Veloso said, crying.
(This is the day that I have been waiting for the most.)
Veloso spent almost two years in prison after the Indonesian government agreed that she be returned to the Philippines.

Among those who met Veloso were her lawyers from Migrante and the National Union of People’s Lawyers, who helped her with her case after she was arrested in Indonesia in 2010 on charges of drug trafficking.
Heroin was found in a suitcase that someone asked her to bring.
She was scheduled for execution in 2015, but President Benigno “Noynoy” Aquino III interceded for her with the Indonesian government.
Indonesia transferred custody of Veloso to the Philippines in 2024. –NB, GMA News
