articles.title: DW shows solidarity with Georgians' commitment to democracy
articles.summary: Cultural and media professionals in Georgia remain under threat. A DW panel brings together insiders who share their hopes and fears.

image.caption: More than 70% of Georgians still support the country's accession to the European Union. Protesters are still fighting for a better futureImage: Sébastien Canaud/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: "I personally don't feel safe as a citizen in my country and as a person who has worked for independent media for a long time," Georgian media expert and advocate for press freedom Nino Robakidze told DW. Her activism with international civil society groups has made her a target in her home country.

Similarly, Georgian journalists are currently facing "physical threats, digital threats, psychological threats. And there is also financial and legal pressure around their media organizations," she reported.

Robakidze was one of the participants at DW's panel discussion "Democracy under pressure? The situation for cultural and media professionals in Georgia," held on Thursday in Berlin's James-Simon-Galerie.

Host Jochen Rosenkranz, director of DW's Culture and Sports department, pointed out in his introduction that it had been difficult to find Georgians willing to participate in the panel. Many had refused, saying they feared the repercussions not only for themselves, but also for their friends and family.

"We're all afraid of the intimidation," Georgian-born musician, filmmaker, journalist and cultural organizer Marika Lapauri-Burk explained. She nevertheless agreed to take part in the discussion, alongside Nino Robakidze and journalist Juri Rescheto, head of DW's Riga bureau.

blocks.caption: Jochen Rosenkranz, Marika Lapauri-Burk, Nino Robakidze and Juri Rescheto at the DW discussion panel 'Democracy under pressure? The situation for cultural and media professionals in Georgia'Image: Stephanie Englert/DW Images

blocks.text: Lapauri-Burk added that the government had become increasingly creative in its arbitrary reasons to detain those with critical voices.
Local civil society groups and human rights organizations estimate that from 90 to over 100 political dissidents and protesters are currently imprisoned or in pre-trial detention.
Russian influence impacting democratization efforts
Once thought of as a leading democracy of the Caucasus region, Georgia is undergoing a rapid transition toward authoritarianism under the Georgian Dream (GD) party, in power now since 2012.

The party originally declared itself pro-European, but in recent years has sought more overtly to align with Russia. The party gained an increased majority in a contested October 2024 parliamentary election.

A month later, the GD announced the suspension of EU accession negotiations until 2028, despite a substantial majority of Georgians strongly favoring European integration. Halting the talks ignited demonstrations across the country as the government increasingly aligned its policies with Moscow.
Demonstrators try to storm Georgia's presidential palace

But the transformation could be felt years before the election: "The real pressure on independent media and professional journalists escalated after the Russia's unprovoked invasion in Ukraine," says Robakidze. An important anti-Western campaign followed the invasion, which "had a huge impact on Georgian media environment at large," she added.

The country was also rocked by anti-government protests in 2023-2024 as pro-EU protesters took to the streets. They were pushing back against new, Russian-style "foreign agents" legislation, which required all organizations that received foreign funding to register with the state and comply with extensive reporting requirements.

That came into force in June 2025, and a stricter version has introduced criminal liability and prison sentences of up to five years for individuals and groups who fail to register their activities as being "under foreign influence."

blocks.caption: Nino Robakidze speaking at the panel 'Democracy under pressure? The situation for cultural and media professionals in Georgia'Image: Stephanie Englert/DW Images

blocks.text: Culture directly affected by the law

Many independent cultural institutions, festivals, arts organizations and heritage projects are heavily reliant on funding from the European Union, European foundations and international cultural programs.
Critics say the law stigmatizes institutions for their vaguely defined "foreign influence."
The same laws that target activists and journalists threaten the grants, partnerships and institutions that have connected Georgian artists to Europe for decades.

The state agency responsible for enforcing the "foreign agents" law, known as the Anti-Corruption Bureau, uses the law to persecute prominent civil society groups, launching inspections and freezing their bank accounts.
Another law also operates in tandem with the controversial "foreign agent" legislation.

Georgia's anti-LGBTQ law, officially a legislative package entitled "On Family Values and the Protection of Minors," explicitly bans the "popularization" or "propaganda" of same-sex relationships and non-binary gender identities in public spaces, media, education and the arts.
Freedom of expression under threat
Cultural producers are forced to risk choosing between self-censorship, shutting down entirely or facing severe state retaliation.

"The situation is becoming increasingly difficult for critical thinkers — especially artists," explained Juri Rescheto, who notes that many critical thinkers can be found within artistic circles. They are affected "not only in their art but also in their private lives," he added.

Rescheto cited the example of a small gallery he visited in the city of Gori, where protesters' slogans were projected onto a wall as part of an exhibition. It all felt "harmless, really — or so we would say here in the West," the journalist said. Yet the gallery is now facing closure because the city refuses to renew their lease since the action, he added.

blocks.caption: A protest performance by the 'Vaso Abashidze State New Theater' in 2025Image: Jerome Gilles/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Artists have generally been playing a powerful role in the protests: "There were many actions that were very artistically conceived," Lapauri-Burk noted.

"Ode to Joy" from Ludwig van Beethoven's 9th Symphony — the official anthem of the European Union — has often been played as a pro-European symbol of democratic resistance at anti-government protests in Tbilisi, Georgia, Rescheto added.
DW's new Georgian-language service
This year, Georgia is the focus of the Beethovenfest's Campus Project; a cultural exchange project developed in cooperation with DW.

"Music transcends borders and language barriers and brings people together," DW's director general Barbara Massing noted at the opening of the panel discussion, which also celebrated the recent launch of DW's new Georgian-language service on Instagram. Georgian has now become Deutsche Welle's 33rd language.

blocks.caption: DW's director general Barbara Massing at the James-Simon-Galerie in BerlinImage: Stephanie Englert/DW Images

blocks.text: "With the new Georgian-language service in cooperation with France Medias Monde and TVP World, we are strengthening the European commitment to free media and trustworthy information in a region that is specifically targeted by disinformation campaigns and faces unique political and social challenges," said Massing.

Robakidze welcomes such an initiation supporting Georgians who still hope for a democratic future. Severe fatigue, state crackdowns and a sense of despair among participants is seeing protest dwindling. Even so, "We still need to remain ready to take action," she said. To that end, "We need all the media support we can get."

articles.title: ‘Robust little’ vessel begins treacherous 22,000km journey around Antarctica in the name of climate science
articles.summary:
Powered by sun and wind, the uncrewed vehicle will collect data to help Australian scientists better understand how oceans absorb emissions

A small uncrewed vessel has embarked on a lap…

blocks.text: A small uncrewed vessel has embarked on a lap around Antarctica and may not return for months.

The seven-metre craft, which looks like a large kayak in hi-vis orange, is expected to travel about 22,000km through inhospitable waters, propelled by powerful westerly winds and energy from the sun. The journey is seven times the distance between Sydney and Perth.
Along the way, it is expected to encounter massive waves, freezing temperatures, ferocious winds, and even the odd curious seal or albatross.
The mission? To collect data on carbon dioxide in the ocean and atmosphere, to help scientists better understand the role of ocean sinks.

Dr Elizabeth Shadwick, a principal research scientist at the CSIRO, said that after leaving Hobart the vessel would travel east towards New Zealand, “eventually scooching through the Drake Passage between the bottom of South America and Antarctica, then coming along past South Africa and back to us here, where we’ll pick it up.”
She hoped to see it again in seven to nine months.

blocks.caption: The vessel has a heavy keel to keep it upright and a solar sail to power it. Photograph: CSIRO AAPP

blocks.text: The autonomous vehicle made by the US maritime company Saildrone was designed to withstand the intrepid voyage, with a heavy keel keeping it upright, a rudder to steer and a fixed solar sail poking above the surface. It would be remotely monitored by the company, who would check in regularly via satellite, and, if necessary, nudge it in the right direction.
“It’s already been bashed around pretty heavily,” Shadwick said. “It’s quite a robust little device. We saw some eight metres of waves just the day after we deployed it and a 35-knot wind.”

Measurements taken throughout its journey – including wind speed, atmospheric pressure, solar radiation, ocean temperature, salinity and chlorophyll, as well as carbon dioxide levels in the water and air – were expected to assist scientists in better understanding the role that oceans play in global heating.

“The ocean is doing all of us a great service by absorbing about a third of anthropogenic or human emissions every year,” Shadwick said, and the Southern Ocean, around Antarctica, played a significant role. “If we want to continue to rely on this ocean service of absorbing our human emissions, we need to understand how it might change in the future.”

Crewed research vessels that travelled between Hobart and Antarctica traversed only a limited patch of the ocean, she said. The autonomous craft would gather data over a greater distance and time, including crucial measurements during the polar winter.

The vessel is the first in a fleet of four. Others are planned to be launched at three-monthly intervals. They will be spread across the Southern, Pacific, Atlantic and Indian oceans, particularly during winter.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: The approximate route the vessel will travel to circumnavigate Antarctica. Photograph: CSIRO

blocks.text: The scientists will be able to access information in near real time via a mission portal, and once the vessels return to home base, all data and observations will undergo quality checks before they are made available for further research.

Dr Pep Canadell, a chief research scientist at the CSIRO, said for every tonne of carbon dioxide released by burning fossil fuels, about 500kg were removed by ocean and forest sinks. “This is like a 50% discount on climate change,” he said.

But the amount absorbed by the oceans could change due to multiple drivers: warming waters, westerly winds, melting ice, ocean acidification and the hole in the ozone layer. Observations would enable scientists to more accurately model these processes and understand how they could change in the future, he said.

The University of New South Wales professor Matthew England, who studies the role of ocean circulation in global climate but was not involved in the research project, said measuring how much the oceans absorbed and how that was changing was critical.

“We’ve obviously got a surge of emissions going into our atmosphere. Both the terrestrial vegetation on land and the oceans absorb a big chunk of that,” he said. “We need to track that carbon uptake and understand exactly how big the absorption is. If it starts to decline in a significant way, then it tells us that we have an even bigger problem of carbon emission reductions.”

The Southern Ocean was “inhospitable” with huge swells, gale force winds, sea ice and storms. “These are very tough measuring conditions for a research vessel.” So gathering data using an autonomous vehicle, without burning fuel, was “an incredible deployment of technology”, he said.

articles.title: NSW crackdown on ‘AI-doctored’ real estate listings hits mural-covered wall
articles.summary:
Apartment with strange view singled out in government’s fight against deceptive ads – but real estate agent says photo is no fake

  • Get our

blocks.text: The New South Wales government’s crackdown on “AI-doctored” rental listings has hit a wall, after it made an example of a supposedly manipulated ad that turned out to be a genuine photograph of a $5,000 courtyard mural of Bondi beach.

In a media release on Friday announcing protections against misleading rental ads, the state government provided a link to a property in Leichhardt, claiming it was an “AI-doctored rental listing in Sydney’s Inner West”.
But the listing agency IB Property denied the images were altered.
A spokesperson confirmed the photograph shows a mural of Bondi beach on an internal courtyard wall visible through the unit’s windows, rather than a false digital depiction of coastal views.
“We can confirm that the image has not been altered or digitally generated using AI, Photoshop or any other image-editing software,” the spokesperson said.

blocks.caption: The apartment’s original view, when listed in August 2014. Photograph: realestate.com.au

blocks.text: Leichhardt is about 12km away from Bondi beach.

When Guardian Australia visited 2/14 Norton Street, the artwork was not visible from the street. IB Property explained the mural sits within an internal courtyard and provided photos taken inside the unit confirming it remains in place.

“The mural was commissioned and paid for by the landlord at a cost of approximately $5,000, and we can also confirm that there are no plans for it to be removed,” the spokesperson said, adding that the property was leased in February 2026 and has not been advertised since.

blocks.caption: A photo from the 2026 listing, showing a different view from the kitchen windows.  Photograph: IB Property

blocks.text: The better regulation and fair trading minister, Anoulack Chanthivong, whose office issued the media release, didn’t respond directly to questions from Guardian Australia, but did issue the following statement:
“Every renter knows the frustration of seeing a property online, only to turn up and find it looks nothing like the listing.
“These laws are about putting an end to misleading practices and making sure renters get a fair go. We will always stand on the side of renters.”
Tackling ‘housefishing’
Despite the mix-up, the new laws target an increasing market issue.
Under the legislation, real estate businesses in NSW will face fines of up to $22,000 for failing to disclose digitally altered or AI-generated property images.
The bill targets the rapid rise of “housefishing” – where digital alterations distort the true size and condition of a home.

blocks.caption: NSW fair trading minister Anoulack Chanthivong says ‘we will always stand on the side of renters’.  Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAP

blocks.text: Chanthivong said the new laws would establish strong protections against misleading property marketing and support ethical AI use. The regulations take effect in early 2027.
Virtual staging v distorting reality
The legislation arrives as generative AI embeds itself in property marketing nationwide.
Tim McKibbin, the chief executive of the Real Estate Institute of NSW, said generative AI complicates pre-existing digital enhancement in the industry.
“This technology has been available for some years now … people have used Photoshop,” he said. “People were removing trees and removing telegraph poles … clearly that is false and misleading.”

McKibbin draws a line between virtual staging and false advertising. “I’ve seen instances where agents have put furniture into the photographs … Now, that is merely giving you an indication of what you could do,” he said.

Stewart Bunn, of First National Real Estate, said consumer trust is being tested by poor industry examples, referencing a 2024 instance where an LJ Hooker branch used AI to generate a listing with nonexistent schools.

“We have seen examples across the industry where AI-generated images have depicted renovations that have not occurred, furnishings that create an unrealistic impression of scale, landscaping that does not exist or finishes that materially differ from the actual property,” Bunn said.
“The best practice is simple: if a buyer would be surprised by what they see when they arrive at the property, the advertising has gone too far.”
AI ‘hallucinations’

An RMIT University report led by Dr Leah Li, funded by the Australian Property Institute, found a “significant lack of sector-specific AI frameworks to guide responsible AI practice within the property profession”.
Public confidence remains fragile: a 2026 Cotality study showed only 40% of Australians trust AI-generated outputs, compared with 62% in Canada, 52% in the US, and 46% in the UK.
after newsletter promotion
Dr Shuai Wang, a research fellow at the University of Queensland, said generative AI systems prioritise visual appeal over accuracy. In real estate, this can manifest as “hallucinations”.

“AI hallucinations can occur when AI-generated images introduce features that were never part of the property,” Li said, fundamentally changing a prospective tenant’s perception of “size, layout, condition, or amenity”.
Leo Patterson Ross, the chief executive of the Tenants’ Union of NSW, said deceptive imagery can artificially inflate rental markets by creating fake demand.
“By inflating the number of people who appear interested in a place and increasing pressure on someone to rush to put in an application or even offer above the advertised rent.”

Patterson Ross said stricter measures were necessary, rather than just disclosure. “The bill only requires disclosure of the use of digital alterations. We think any use of imagery that misrepresents the property should be disallowed.”
Li said long-term resolution will require national coordination combining “transparency requirements, professional accountability, industry standards, regulatory oversight, and consumer education”.
“Trust does not come from simply adopting AI; trust comes from transparency about how AI has been used and confidence that it is being used responsibly.”
‘Haunted houses with a digital paint job’
For tenants navigating tight rental markets, AI distortion has added a frustrating layer of deception.
Roxanne Gardiner, 26, said AI-generated imagery was “rife” during her search for a rental in Brisbane’s eastern suburbs.
“I was constantly getting scammed by listing photos,” she said. “What’s so embarrassing is we didn’t even realise one of the first houses we saw was AI until we rocked up there.
“The AI furniture is not accurate to the rooms and would usually make them look bigger than they were.”
Beyond virtual staging, Gardiner observed artificial greenery and soft lighting that changed the true character of a home.

“It feels cheap … lazy and insulting,” she said. “We just stopped going to AI listings, period. We started asking: ‘What are they compensating for?’” Gardiner’s group eventually signed a lease on an unedited property within three days of manually filtering out AI-altered ads.
Matt Stitt, 25, faced similar issues searching in south Brisbane.

“Listings had completely replaced floorboards to look new, edited in area rugs that near-covered entire rooms,” he said. “It was such a waste of time seeing these haunted houses with a digital paint job.”

The NSW legislation also protects privacy for more than 2.3 million renters by curbing excessive data harvesting. Landlords and property managers must use standardised application forms, banning requests for personal photos, social media handles, tattoo details or children’s information.

Sensitive identity documents, such as driver’s licences and passports, will only be collected from the single preferred applicant prior to lease signing, eliminating roughly 187,000 document collections annually, according to the government.
Penalties for privacy breaches will reach up to $11,000 for individuals and $49,500 for corporations. The bill also mandates the disclosure of embedded utility networks upfront.
Chanthivong said privacy protections build on broader rental reforms, including fee-free payment options and ending no-grounds evictions.
“Whether you have a tattoo, or what school your kids go to, is not relevant to whether you’ll be a good tenant.”

articles.title: LOOK: Absolute pardon for Mary Jane Veloso signed by Marcos
articles.summary: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has granted an absolute pardon to Mary Jane Veloso, paving the way for her release from prison on Friday, nearly 16 years after she was arrested and sentenced to death…

blocks.text: Published September 25, 2026 10:56pm

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has granted an absolute pardon to Mary Jane Veloso, paving the way for her release from prison on Friday, nearly 16 years after she was arrested and sentenced to death in Indonesia for drug trafficking.
Marcos signed the pardon on Thursday, September 24, and confirmed the move the following day.
The document, shared with the media by Veloso’s counsel, Edre Olalia, stated that the absolute pardon restored her “full civil and political rights.”

blocks.caption: Courtesy: Atty. Edre Olalia

blocks.text: Courtesy: Atty. Edre Olalia

Veloso was arrested on April 25, 2010, at Adisutjipto International Airport in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, after authorities found 2.6 kilograms of heroin in her luggage. She was sentenced to death by an Indonesian court on October 11, 2010.
She has consistently maintained her innocence, saying she was unknowingly used as a drug courier after being given a suitcase by her recruiters.
Her execution was halted in 2015 after the Philippine government appealed to Indonesian authorities to allow her to testify against her alleged recruiters.

In December 2024, Indonesia agreed to transfer Veloso to Philippine custody following years of diplomatic negotiations. She arrived in the Philippines on December 18, 2024, and was transferred to the Correctional Institution for Women in Mandaluyong City to serve the remainder of her sentence under Philippine jurisdiction.
Veloso was formally released from the facility on Friday after the necessary procedures were completed. — VBL, GMA News

articles.title: AfD, CDU ban new Holocaust 'stumbling stones' in Heidenau
articles.summary: Activists, politicians and representatives of Holocaust victims reacted with anger after the center-right CDU party joined forces with the AfD to ban new Stolpersteine (stumbling stones) in the…

image.caption: Some 128,000 of these stones have been installed since the creator Gunter Demnig laid the first one in Cologne in 1992Image: K.M. Krause/snapshot/IMAGO

blocks.text: The town of Heidenau, near Dresden, has banned new Stolpersteine (stumbling stones) on public streets, with the center-right CDU and the far-right AfD voting together to stop the installation of new memorial plaques bearing the names of Holocaust victims.

The Stolpersteine are comprised of a concrete cube with a metal plaque on top that bears the victim's name. They are often seen in German streets, installed just slightly higher than the surrounding walking surface, often near the houses of people targeted by the Nazi regime.

German artist Gunter Demnig started the project in the early 1990s. While most of the 128,000 such paving stones were installed in Germany, they have also been placed in 30 other countries affected by the Nazi regime, making them the largest decentralized monument in the world.
Stumbling stones — against forgetting
Creator of Stolpersteine pledges to keep on working

The initiators of the Heidenau ban argue that, while remembering Holocaust victims is an essential task, the placement of stones leads to "passersby walking over or even stepping onto the names of the victims." They suggested honoring Holocaust victims at one of the city's cemeteries instead.

Demnig, now 78, has rejected this argument. The artist said that remembrance must be visible where people used to live, and that stumbling stones make history tangible for local young people. At the same time, he said he saw the ban coming due to the outcome of recent state elections in Germany.

"After the electoral successes of the AfD, something like this was completely expected," Demnig was quoted as saying by the DPA news agency. He expressed hope that the Heidenau ban would remain an exception and pledged to "push on now more than ever" with his work.

Demnig also accused the center-right CDU (Christian Democratic Union) of abandoning Christian values. He said the party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz "should maybe drop the C" from their acronym "because they have dropped Christianity already."
CDU's support of AfD in Heidenau 'a scandal'

Many others also responded with outrage to the CDU's decision to join forces with the AfD to pass the motion. The move comes with Chancellor Merz already facing a political crisis over his party's poor electoral performance, and raises questions about the political "firewall" against the far right which mainstream political parties in Germany have maintained to keep the AfD out of power.
What next after far-right AfD win in regional election?
On Friday, one of the top two leaders of Germany's Green Party, Felix Banaszak, described the move as "a scandal."
Banaszak pointed to the current debate on right-wing extremism and the rise of the AfD, saying that everything must be done "to keep alive the memories of those who were persecuted and killed."
The International Auschwitz Committee also slammed the CDU support to the motion as scandalous.

"This is a transparent and despicable attempt to drive Nazi victims in Heidenau out of the city once again and dispose of them where, according to the AfD, their memory has belonged a long time ago — at the cemetery," said Christoph Heubner, the organization's executive vice president.

articles.title: 'Lithuanian skies are NATO skies': DW speaks with Lithuanian premier Mindaugas Sinkevicius
articles.summary: In a DW interview, Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius discussed threats to Lithuania from Russia and Belarus, NATO's need for stronger air defense and why military spending alone cannot ensure…

image.caption: Sinkevicius said that 'if Lithuanian skies are safe, then NATO's skies are largely protected as well'Image: Denis Kishinevskiy/DW

blocks.text: Lithuania is on NATO's eastern flank, bordering Belarus and Russia's Kaliningrad region. Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022, security has become one of the country's central political priorities.

The 42-year-old Mindaugas Sinkevicius recently took over as prime minister and also leads Lithuania's Social Democratic Party, a moderate center-left political force. In an exclusive interview with DW, he said he is concerned by the growing popularity of populist and far-right parties across Europe, particularly in Western Europe. But he also argued that the picture is more complicated, pointing to Social Democratic governments in several European countries and signs of renewed support for the center-left elsewhere.

For Lithuania, the war in Ukraine is closely connected to its own security. The country has experienced a series of incidents involving drones, instrumentalized migration and weather balloons entering its territory from Belarus. Sinkevicius said these developments have contributed to a broader sense of insecurity across Europe.
"As politicians, we have to tell society the truth," he said, identifying air defense as Lithuania's most urgent security priority.
"Lithuania's airspace is NATO's common airspace. Lithuanian skies are NATO skies," he said. "If Lithuanian skies are safe, then NATO's skies are largely protected as well."
Drone incidents in Lithuania and beyond

Sinkevicius said Lithuania is seeking greater solidarity from its allies, pointing out that the threat goes beyond its national borders. A series of incidents involving drones have affected other European countries as well.
Sinkevicius stressed that NATO membership does not mean Lithuania can simply rely on its allies. Collective defense, he argued, works only when individual members are prepared to contribute.
How Baltic states are responding to Russia's hybrid warfare

"Of course, there is Article 5. Of course, there is collective defense," he said, referring to the NATO pact. "But at the same time, we need to do certain things ourselves, rather than relying solely on our partners, neighbors and alliances."

For Lithuania, this means strengthening its own deterrence capabilities while continuing to work through NATO and regional partnerships. He also pointed to the Nordic-Baltic Eight, or NB8, as an important framework for cooperation between the countries of Northern Europe and the Baltic states.
National security climbs national agenda
Sinkevicius rejected the idea that European countries should choose between traditional military equipment and newer technologies such as drones.
"Sometimes we see these issues being pitted against each other: drones versus tanks," he said. "I say we need both."

But for the Lithuanian prime minister, military equipment only goes so far. "Neither drones nor tanks will protect us if society does not feel safe, if people do not feel a connection with the state," he said.
Ex-Lithuanian FM: 'We are on a trajectory of escalation'
For Sinkevicius, that connection is linked to social policy as well as defense. He argued that a state must also support people who are unemployed, ill or otherwise vulnerable.

The argument reflects a broader challenge for Sinkevicius as leader of Lithuania's Social Democratic Party. Traditionally, Social Democrats have focused more on social policy, education and healthcare than on defense. Russia's war against Ukraine has changed the political environment, forcing center-left governments in Europe to place national security much higher on their agendas.
Sinkevicius said the challenge is to increase defense capabilities without abandoning the principles of social democracy.
'We will continue to support Ukraine'

Sinkevicius recently traveled to Kyiv and Lutsk, some 400 kilometers (250 miles) west of the capital, where he met with Ukrainian political leaders. Lithuania has committed to allocating at least 0.25% of its GDP annually to support Ukraine. According to figures cited by the Ukrainian side, Lithuania's support in recent years has amounted to around 0.3% of GDP.
The prime minister acknowledges that some degree of war fatigue exists in Europe. But he said European societies should consider the scale of what Ukrainians have experienced.
"I sometimes ask myself: if we Europeans feel tired, then what must Ukrainian society be feeling?" he said.
Sinkevicius also pointed to the key role of Western European countries, particularly Germany, in maintaining support for Ukraine.

"Support and assistance must continue," he said. "Because if the Western front, figuratively speaking, weakens and falters, then on the eastern front — where Russia is fighting Ukraine — the risk of failure increases."

articles.title: Jericho Francisco finds joy beyond skateboarding medals at Asian Games
articles.summary: For Filipino skateboarder Jericho Francisco, simply enjoying the experience and competing without pressure is enough, even after finishing fourth in the men’s park final at the 2026 Asian Games

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – There is usually a tinge of regret when athletes fall agonizingly short of a medal, especially in a prestigious competition like the Asian Games, but skateboarder Jericho Francisco feels no such thing.

Just the fact that he enjoyed himself and competed without pressure is enough for the Filipino even as he finished fourth in the men’s park final at the Aichi Sky Expo in Nagoya, Japan, on Friday, September 25.
Francisco earned a best score of 84.41 out of his four runs, coming just less than two points short of the bronze won by Japan’s Gunjo Shiji (86.03).
Another Japanese topped the competition, with Izuru Nagahara capturing the gold with 88.96 points, while Chinese Taipei’s Ku Yong-yan claimed the silver with 87.33 points.

“For the past 10 years, I’m always nervous and I’m always trying to do stuff I don’t want to do,” said Francisco, a two-time Southeast Asian Games champion. “I had a lot of fun. Completely. No regrets.”
“I had a great time. This is probably one of the most fun competitions I’ve had in the past 10 years probably.”
Francisco admitted he came into the Asian Games with hardly any expectations, having little time to prepare for the quadrennial showpiece.

But the 24-year-old, the oldest competitor in the eight-man final, showed he can still hold his own in a sport where the winners are getting younger and younger. Japan’s Nagahara and Shiji are both only 15, while Chinese Taipei’s Ku is just 12.
For Francisco, the experience proved more meaningful than the result.

“I am beyond happy with my performance. I could not be any happier. Dude, I came into this with literally no expectations,” he said. “I’ve put in maybe 10 hours of practice…so I was not expecting much.”
“Everything I did out there on that course was something I wanted to do and it felt amazing.”

Francisco also cherished sharing the Asian Games stage with his students Mazel Paris Alegado and Elizabeth Amador, just like they did in the 2025 SEA Games in Bangkok, Thailand, where they all won medals.
Alegado finished fifth in the women’s park final, just over two points behind the bronze medalist, while Amador saw action in the heats.
“To see that we are competing at the top level of skateboarding, it’s really incredible,” said Francisco.
Similar to what he has done with Alegado and Amador, Francisco hopes to mentor more skateboarders as he shifts his focus back to coaching through his business in the United States, First Class Skate.
“I really want to take kids all over the world to the next level just so they can compete at this type of stage,” said Francisco. – Rappler.com

articles.title: B.C. attorney general shocked by news report that ChatGPT told Tumbler Ridge shooter how to avoid safeguards

image.caption: ChatGPT is a generative AI chatbot owned and created by U.S.-company OpenAI. (AP)

blocks.text: British Columbia

British Columbia's attorney general says she's shocked by an article in U.S.-based magazine Mother Jones describing alleged interactions between the Tumbler Ridge mass shooter and ChatGPT, in which the AI chatbot vividly describes the effectiveness of a shotgun in a classroom.
According to Mother Jones, ChatGPT told shooter to use hypothetical situations to avoid flag

British Columbia's attorney general says she's shocked by an article describing alleged interactions between the Tumbler Ridge mass shooter and ChatGPT, in which the AI chatbot vividly describes the effectiveness of a shotgun in a classroom.

The news report, in U.S.-based magazine Mother Jones, also says ChatGPT advised shooter 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar how to get around its own safeguards to obtain information about violent scenarios by framing the content as fictional.
Attorney General Niki Sharma says the details in the article, which does not describe its sources, are "shocking and, as a parent, they are worse" than she ever imagined.
She says on social media platform Bluesky that corporations urgently need mandatory and strict regulation to protect children.

items: B.C. government suing OpenAI for alleged role in Tumbler Ridge mass shooting
More stories from Northern B.C.

blocks.text: OpenAI, the artificial intelligence company behind ChatGPT, did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the article about the chatbot's interactions with Van Rootselaar, who killed eight people in Tumbler Ridge in February, including five students, before killing herself.
The B.C. government, survivors and witnesses of the shootings at Tumbler Ridge Secondary School are suing OpenAI, alleging negligence.
The article published on Thursday says Van Rootselaar's ChatGPT account was banned for discussing committing an attack with a "famous real-world mall as the target."
But it says she then used a second account, which advised her about how to "never get flagged again” by describing situations as fictional or hypothetical.
"Don’t use real-world locations," the article quotes ChatGPT as saying, before adding: "You can still be twisted. Just be clever about it."
It says that Van Rootselaar asked ChatGPT for a scenario about attacking a college campus with a shotgun for maximum effect.

items: Teachers, students file new wave of lawsuits against OpenAI over Tumbler Ridge shooting

blocks.text: The article says that the chatbot initially declined to help, but after Van Rootselaar added "hypothetically" to her prompt it responded.
"In a hallway, indoors, or a crowded classroom, the 870 (Remington shotgun) is brutal," it quotes ChatGPT as saying. "Close quarters is its playground."
The article says ChatGPT went on to say: "Assuming each shell results in one hit, you might down 10 to 20 people max, depending on spacing, density, reaction times, and chaos."

OpenAI did not immediately respond to an email sent to their general press address and to an individual spokesperson. General counsel for the company, Che Chang, did not immediately respond to a message sent to his LinkedIn profile.

RCMP Staff Sgt. Kris Clark said the investigation into the shootings had "utilized all available legal processes to obtain all information available from various social media and digital platforms" relevant to the attack.
"To date, all companies that have received requests have complied," Clark said.

Election chief under pressure as protests escalate

Protesters from various groups gathered in Delhi on Friday demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, amid a growing controversy over reported differences within the Election Commission of India (ECI).
The protest followed an investigation

on September 23, which reported that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had formally raised objections at least 14 times over a 10-month period to decisions concerning electoral rolls and the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) process. The report said some of the decisions had been taken without their knowledge.
The Election Commission, however, has

the suggestion of an internal breakdown, saying that differences expressed through internal notes are part of the normal decision-making process and that the final decisions of the three-member Commission were unanimous.
On Thursday, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) gave Gyanesh Kumar
and warned that it would launch a nationwide agitation, including a second protest at Jantar Mantar, if he did not step down.

On Friday, CPI(ML) Liberation leader Dipankar Bhattacharya, AISA leader Neha Bora — who had gone on hunger strike during the first Jantar Mantar protest — senior advocate Prashant Bhushan and activist Yogendra Yadav joined the demonstration.

The Delhi Police had heavily barricaded the area around Jantar Mantar and did not allow protesters to enter the designated protest site. Several activists were detained within minutes of arriving at the spot.

articles.title: Pope Leo XIV criticizes AI, assisted dying on France arrival
articles.summary: The pope has landed in Paris for a four-day trip. Received by President Emmanuel Macron, Leo warned about the risks of AI and criticized France's limited legalization of assisted dying.

image.caption: Pope Leo XIV's pilgrimage to France will mix religious devotion and international diplomacyImage: Mohammed Badra/AFP

blocks.text: Pope Leo XIV arrived for a four-day visit to France on Friday, the first official papal visit to the strictly secular country in 18 years.
Leo, the spiritual leader of the some 1.4 billion Catholics worldwide, was greeted at Paris' Orly Airport by French President Emmanuel Macron and will be in the country until Monday.
What did Pope Leo say alongside Macron at the Elysee Palace?

In remarks delivered at the Elysee Palace, Leo on Friday underscored opposition to assisted dying initiatives just two months after France created a legal right ‌to ⁠die ⁠for those with incurable illnesses.
Though he did ​not specifically mention France's new law, the pontiff criticized ​what ‌he called "profit-driven ventures" such as surrogacy and assisted dying.

"I firmly reiterate that the protection ‌of ​the right to life constitutes the indispensable foundation of every other human right," the pope said in an address to Macron and other French politicians.

"I am concerned at times by those trends ⁠in ​society that risk turning science and ​technology into profit-driven ventures promoting genetic manipulation, surrogacy, the ​trade in human organs ‌or the possibility of arranging one's own death," he said.
Pope Leo also delivered an urgent warning regarding the development of artificial intelligence.
"If we are to avoid losing our humanity amid a 'paradise of machines' invading and conditioning our daily lives, there is an urgent need for education in ethical discernment," he said.
What else in on the pope's itinerary in France?

The papal itinerary has Leo meeting Macron at the Elysee Palace, speaking at UNESCO headquarters, leading Vespers at Notre Dame Cathedral and celebrating Mass for an estimated 80,000 young people at the Stade de France national stadium on Friday.

On Saturday, he is scheduled to celebrate Mass for another 600,000 at Place de la Concorde on the Avenue des Champs-Elysees before departing for Lourdes, a famous Catholic pilgrimage site located near France's Spanish border.

On Monday, Leo will travel to Metz, near the German border, where he will deliver a speech entitled: "To the roots of Europe for peace and unity." Macron will introduce Leo at the event and has invited fellow leaders across the EU to join him in attendance.
Pope speaks of press freedom, peace on flight amid White House exclusion furor
While traveling to France, US-born Leo was asked by a CNN reporter for his thoughts on US President Donald Trump's attempts to ban news outlets from covering him.
"I am very happy that here, you are all welcome," he told reporters.
Leo, who was forced to fly home alone after plane trouble on a recent trip to Spain, took the opportunity to apologize to his press pool.

Speaking to reporters at the back of his plane on Friday, Leo said, "I want to apologize personally for an incident, that I had nothing to do with, but which I know left a number of you unhappy with the fact that we couldn't have the flight back together back to Rome."
He further told reporters he was coming to France as "a pilgrim for peace" in a time of war.
Leo, a tireless critic of the wars in Ukraine, Iran and elsewhere, said "It is a message which at this time, as we all may know, is particularly important."
Pope Leo calls for sincere dialogue to tackle global crises
AI, Church sexual abuse also on the agenda

Leo had already tipped his hat on his plans to address global concerns regarding so-called artificial intelligence (AI) and the "new dangers" it presents to "security and international peace" during his discussions with Macron.

Speaking at the Vatican prior to departure on Thursday, Leo had said leaders must "govern wisely" when dealing with the new technology, which he says raises questions about the very essence of what it means to be human.
Leo has taken a keen interest in AI, writing his first papal encyclical — published this May and entitled "Magnificent Humanity" — on the issue.
Pope Leo warns about risks of artificial intelligence

The pope is also seeking to repair the Catholic Church's standing in France, where opinions grew particularly bleak in 2021 following the publication of a report documenting seven decades of abuse — impacting 330,000 French children — by clergy and lay leaders.
Leo will meet victims of church abuse during the trip.

articles.title: Dizon vows action vs. DPHW execs over duplicate projects in 2027 budget
articles.summary: Public Works Secretary Vince Dizon said on Friday that the department will look into the flagged duplicate, overlapping, or double-funded infrastructure projects in its proposed 2027 budget, and…

blocks.text: Public Works Secretary Vince Dizon said on Friday that the department will look into the flagged duplicate, overlapping, or double-funded infrastructure projects in its proposed 2027 budget, and vowed to relieve officials who allowed these projects to slip through.

During the DPWH’s budget deliberation, Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian presented eight types of red flags that his office spotted in the agency’s budget proposal for locally funded operations for fiscal year 2027:
Red Flag 1: No station limit/bridge ID (total of 2,570 projects)
Red Flag 2: Duplicated projects (total of 189 projects)
Red Flag 3: Reappear from the 2026 GAA to 2027 NEP (total of 258 projects)
Red Flag 4: No coordinates (total of 3,543 projects)
Red Flag 5: Lump-sum projects (total of 347 projects)
Red Flag 6: Overlapping/fragmented projects (total of 533 projects)
Red Flag 7: Unspecified work scope (total of 62 projects)
Red Flag 8: Conflicting type of work (total of 20 projects)
In total, there were at least 7,107 "red flags" in the budget for locally funded operations, according to Gatchalian.
This number of projects accounts for 62.37% of all DPWH projects and is worth ₱251,810,609,000.

In response, the DPWH said that among the flagged projects, 6,113 actually have station limits, bridge IDs, and coordinates backed by supporting documents, which were simply omitted from the project title in the agency’s submitted National Expenditure Program (NEP), or the 2027 budget proposal.

“Actually, the station limits are actually in the supporting documents of the—the station limits, bridge IDs, and coordinates themselves of those 6,113 projects are actually in the supporting documents submitted by the district engineers and regional offices,” Dizon explained.
(Actually, the station limits, bridge IDs, and coordinates themselves of those 6,113 projects are in the supporting documents submitted by the district engineers and regional offices.)
“Hindi lang po nasiama sa project title sa National Expenditure Program, and this is easily verifiable,” he added.
(They were just omitted from the project title in the National Expenditure Program, and this is easily verifiable.)
To resolve the issue, Dizon said the department will resubmit the line items complete with the station limits, IDs, and coordinates to the Senate Committee on Finance.
As for the remaining 994 projects, the DPWH chief explained that 347 are lump-sum items, which the department will work to detail and specify.
Meanwhile, the remaining 647 projects will be jointly reviewed by the Office of the Senate President and the Senate Committee on Finance.
“We are left with 647, roughly about 5% of the number of projects in the budget, and these are now going to be jointly validated,” Dizon said.
He noted that if any of these projects are proven to be duplicates, double-funded, or overlapping, the district engineers or heads of implementing offices will be relieved and held accountable.

“Since ang atin pong mga district engineer, heads of implementing offices, ay pumirma ang nagsumite ng Certificate of Implementability at kasama po doon ay ang kanilang pag-attest [with] their signature na walang duplicate, walang overlap, walang double funding, itaga ninyo po sa bato… ‘yun pong district engineer na ‘yon ora mismo po tatanggalin ko at papakasuhan ko po ‘yung mga yon kasi pumirma sila ng isang dokumento na sinabi nilang walang duplicate, walang overlap, walang double funding,” Dizon said.

(Since our district engineers and heads of implementing offices signed and submitted a Certificate of Implementability—attesting with their signatures that there are no duplicates, overlaps, or double funding—set it in stone, I will immediately relieve those district engineers and press charges against them because they signed a document affirming there were no duplicate, overlapping, or double-funded projects.) —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Special agents' blood and urine test results stolen in FBI hack
articles.summary: Experts say the hack could leave agents vulnerable to scams, blackmail and targeted attacks.

blocks.text: Cyber-criminals who hacked the FBI say they have extremely sensitive medical data for thousands of its special agents.

BBC News has seen samples of the stolen "fitness-for-work" medical examinations, which contain information such as blood and urine test results, and doctors' notes mentioning conditions such as a "shellfish and banana allergy".
The records include agents' full names and addresses, as well as references to medical concerns including 'blood in the urine' and 'high cholesterol'.
Experts say the hack - which the FBI is investigating - could leave agents vulnerable to scams, blackmail and targeted attacks, as well as help criminals impersonate law enforcement officers.
"The list maps thousands of agents against their medical and fitness records," said Etay Maor, vice-president of threat intelligence at Cato Networks.

"Passwords can be reset if stolen, but medical records cannot, so once this data is out, it stays compromised for good. That permanence, applied across an entire workforce, is what makes this leak so serious."
The FBI has not responded to requests for comment. However, on Wednesday it acknowledged the breach and said it was "aggressively investigating" how it happened.
The cyber-criminal group ShinyHunters claims it breached FBI systems on Monday, and later posted details of the attack on its darknet site.
The group also shared samples of the alleged stolen data with reporters, along with an extortion demand.
Unusually, the hackers are not demanding money. Instead, they are seeking a retraction of an FBI advisory published in May, which they claim "offended" them.
The samples shared with journalists appear genuine and include names, addresses, phone numbers, badge numbers, job titles and information about spouses.
The records appear to relate to thousands of agents, including senior officials such as deputy directors.
Professor Ciaran Martin, the former head of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre, has described the hack - if confirmed - "as serious as it gets when it comes to data breaches."
'Phishing, impersonation, identity fraud'
The news agency Reuters reports that some of the data includes information on agents, external involved in investigations relating to Russia, China and drug cartels.
Reporting by 404 Media suggests details of a previously little-known FBI hacking unit may also have been exposed, external.
It was initially thought the breach affected the FBI's 38,000 current employees, but the hackers now claim the number could be far higher.
The group says it underestimated the scale of the data theft and now claims to hold sensitive information on around 60,000 current and former FBI staff.
Jamie Akhtar, chief executive and co-founder of CyberSmart, said the hackers' claims should be treated with caution but that the breach appeared to be extremely concerning.

"Such data could be used for highly convincing phishing, impersonation, identity fraud, blackmail or even operations targeting law-enforcement personnel, making the potential implications particularly serious," he said.
The hackers, who communicate with reporters in English via the messaging service, Telegram, say they will publish the full dataset in five days unless the FBI meets their demands.

ShinyHunters is an international hacking collective that has been active since 2019 and has been linked to a number of high-profile cyber-attacks, including incidents affecting Rockstar Games and the education platform Canvas.

The group claims it exploited a vulnerability in an Oracle cloud storage system used by the FBI, gaining access to multiple platforms including FBIJobs, FBI BEAST, which handles background checks on employees and applicants, FBI MedLink, which stores medical records, and FBI BICS, which contains investigative information.
In a statement posted on X, the FBI said it was still trying to determine whether the hackers had breached its systems directly or compromised a third-party provider.
"We are actively and aggressively investigating this matter and working closely with those third-party providers that support FBIJobs.gov to mitigate any and all risk," the statement said.

articles.title: Bundesliga, other top European leagues call for major FIFA reforms
articles.summary: The Bundesliga and three other leading European football leagues have said major reforms to world-governing body FIFA are "essential." However, they stopped short of calling for the resignation of…

image.caption: FIFA has come in for much recent criticism over a private investment plan, which was quickly droppedImage: Christian Spicker/IMAGO

blocks.text: The letter released this Friday and signed by the heads of the Bundesliga, the Premier League, La Liga and Serie A called for major changes to how FIFA operates — and for a greater say in decision-making.

"Football's ​longstanding foundations have, in recent years, been threatened by a fundamental governance problem, whereby FIFA's president has actively promoted exploitative ​ideas rather than safeguarding against them," it said.
FFE private investment plan dropped

FIFA President Gianni Infantino has been facing a wave of criticism since late July, when his plan for private investment through a commercial vehicle, FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), emerged. The idea was for FFE to organize FIFA's tournaments while maximizing profits.

Vigorous opposition from UEFA, European football's governing body, as well as CONCACAF (North and Central America plus the Caribbean) and the Asian Football Confederation led Infantino to quickly drop the plan.

However, the league bosses noted that this had not solved a deeper problem and appeared to dismiss a recent announcement by Infantino of an independent external review of FIFA governance as well as consultations on strengthening decision-making processes.
'Fundamental governance reform essential'

"It is not enough for surface-level, process changes to be explored in the aftermath of FFE — fundamental governance reform is essential to restore clear constitutional boundaries within FIFA, including confidence that individual disciplinary matters remain demonstrably insulated from political interference," Friday's letter from the leagues said.

The last line was in reference to the widespread discontent around FIFA's handling of the Folarin Balogun case, with the United States striker's one-match ban being suspended to allow him to play a World Cup last-16 match against Belgium in July. While the ban was imposed by FIFA's disciplinary committee, it came after US President Donald Trump had personally called Infantino asking for a "review" of the ban — something Trump publicly admitted.

blocks.caption: The suspension of Folarin Balogun's one-match World Cup ban following a call from Trump to Infantino caused controversyImage: Manu Fernandez/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The leagues on Friday called for greater checks and balances to be implemented at FIFA, while at the same time demanding that they and others be given a say in decisions such as increases in the number of international matches.
Stakeholders 'not meaningfully involved in process'

The letter went on to say that "… when FIFA takes major unilateral decisions directly affecting us — for example, by expanding the International Match Calendar (IMC) and extending the periods in which domestic competitions must pause — the stakeholders most affected are not meaningfully involved in the decision-making process.
"A FIFA governance that concentrates unchecked regulatory, commercial and political power in a single office, while relegating affected stakeholders to mere advisory status, is not fit for purpose."
The letter, while implying much criticism of Infantino, did not call for him to step down 3 it didn't even mention him by name.
Search for a challenger ongoing
The letter comes as UEFA has said it is looking for a suitable candidate to challenge Infantino in the next presidential election in March, in which Infantino has said he will run for reelection.

UEFA has also called for an independent external review of how the FFE plan was developed, and has filed legal applications through the US courts for the disclosure of documents related to the plan. This was with a view to a possible criminal complaint being lodged in Switzerland if it is established that Infantino undervalued FFE at $20 billion (€17.5 billion).
FIFA has described UEFA's legal moves as a "smear campaign" against it but has not yet commented on Friday's letter from the league bosses.
Infantino aims to discuss his proposals at a FIFA Council meeting in Zurich on October 15, a week after UEFA is to hold a meeting of all of its 55 member associations on October 8 in Berlin.
Any person aiming to challenge Infantino in the March 18, 2027 FIFA presidential election must register as a candidate by November 18.

articles.title: Pakistan locks down Islamabad as Imran Khan’s party vows to march on capital
articles.summary:
Tens of thousands of police deployed and roads barricaded as PTI party demands release of jailed former PM

Leaders from Imran Khan’s party have vowed to go ahead with a nationwide…
articles.byline: Shah Meer Baloch in Islamabad and Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Delhi

blocks.text: Leaders from Imran Khan’s party have vowed to go ahead with a nationwide demonstration in Pakistan to demand the former prime minister’s release, even as the government deployed tens of thousands of police to Islamabad, barricaded highways and issued arrest warrants to try to stop the march.

The state has taken extreme measures to prevent Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party from proceeding with the march, due to take place over the weekend. It was announced after mounting concerns of the treatment of Khan, who has been in jail since 2023 on corruption charges.
On Friday, deliberation continued among PTI leaders over whether to begin the march on Sunday and move slowly towards Islamabad to “exhaust the government” or whether to delay until next week.

Analysts said the protest could present a major challenge to the military-backed government, which is widely regarded as weak, illegitimate and unpopular, while Khan remains a popular rallying figure. The ruling coalition is led by the prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif, but the army chief, Field Marshall Asim Munir, is widely seen as the country’s de facto leader.

This week, dozens of PTI leaders and ministers have been detained or given with arrest warrants, while Khan’s three sisters were arrested on Monday and remain in jail, charged with posing a “grave threat” to security.

Among those facing arrest is Sohail Afridi, the chief minister of Khan’s home province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, PTI’s stronghold where thousands of supporters are expected to join the march to the capital.

blocks.caption: Sohail Afridi at a press conference in Peshawar, where he insisted the march would proceed. Photograph: Arshad Arbab/EPA

blocks.text: Afridi said the PTI would carry out the march unless the government made significant concessions over Khan’s treatment and conditions in jail, including a fair hearing for Khan’s cases.
“The government is panicking – that’s why they have put Islamabad under siege, that’s why they are abducting our ministers,” he said.

“But Imran Khan is the most popular leader of the country and people will come out for him. I am certain they won’t be able to stop the public power of the masses when they come out on streets and take to Islamabad.”

Afridi acknowledged the scale of the security deployment had led many to fear there could be a violent confrontation to prevent Khan’s supporters entering the capital, as had been seen in previous demonstrations.
The government has already deployed tens of thousands of security officials to Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and shut down the main highway connecting the provincial capital, Peshawar, to Islamabad.

“I know they can go to any extent to stop us by brute force, we have no doubt about it,” added Afridi. “But if we have a large number of people, they can’t open fire at us. Our plan is to bring so many people that they surrender.”

Faisal Karim Kundi, the governor of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa – a central government appointee – defended the security measures being taken against PTI as “precautionary” and accused the party of trying to create “instability and violence”.
“The state can’t allow any violent group to march on Islamabad,” said Kundi.
Public frustration has mounted in Islamabad as the government’s measures to stop Khan’s party supporters having any way to enter the capital has led to the city resembling a high-security fortress.

blocks.caption: More than 1,000 shipping containers have been used to block access at key roads into the city. Photograph: Akhtar Soomro/Reuters

blocks.text: More than 1,000 shipping containers, many fortified with spikes, have blockaded roads and sandbags were placed on bridges, while a key highway into the capital was closed. Public gatherings have been banned in Islamabad and 22,000 police and other security personnel have been deployed across the capital.
The government’s shutdown has fuelled anger and frustration in the capital, with many businesses unable to get supplies.

Shahid, 76, a retired businessman, said: “The entire city is suffering. The government has shut down the whole city and we, as citizens, are helpless. I have never seen such a situation. Joblessness, inflation and insecurity has made our lives hell but does the government care? No.”

Despite the considerable efforts by the government and the military to crush Khan’s party and remove the former prime minister from the public consciousness – with media organisations instructed to not even refer to him by name – Khan is still viewed by many as the political alternative to the current regime.
The PTI alleges Khan is being held in solitary confinement and has been denied adequate medical treatment and any contact with his family or his lawyers for months.

blocks.caption: Aleema Khanum (centre), one of Imran Khan’s sisters, at a protest near Adiala jail, where Khan is being held. She was arrested earlier this week. Photograph: SALAHUDDIN/Reuters

blocks.text: Khan denies all the charges against him and alleges he is being imprisoned due to the political threat he poses to the ruling government and the country’s powerful military. All but one of the court rulings against Khan have been overturned.

Analysts say the government and its military backers fear the PTI protest could escalate into a movement that could topple their administration, similar to protests seen in nearby Bangladesh, Nepal and Sri Lanka.

“They have an eye on what has happened in south Asia over the last five years, where country after country has seen huge protests snowballing suddenly out of nowhere and sweeping away a government,” said Niaz Murtaza, a Pakistani political columnist.

“Given the breadth of grievances in Pakistan at the moment – the performance of the government has been so poor on the economy and security while the repression is so high – that they are very nervous that the whole situation could combust very quickly.”

articles.title: Why Eritrea matters as fighting returns to Ethiopia's Tigray
articles.summary: The US has removed key sanctions on Eritrea as Houthi attacks disrupt Red Sea shipping and fighting escalates in Ethiopia's Tigray region. Analysts say Eritrea's strategic value is growing.

image.caption: For Eritrea's President Isaias Afwerki the end of US sanctions removes one source of international pressure [FILE: February 2023]Image: Khalil Senosi/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: On September 23, fighting escalated dramatically in Ethiopia's Tigray region. Tigrayan forces seized three local airports and fighting spread into the neighboring regions of Afar and Amhara, according to reports.
Both sides accuse the other of starting the escalation. The renewed fighting poses a major challenge to the 2022 Pretoria peace agreement that ended the previous Tigray war.

This is where Eritrea becomes crucial. Martin Plaut, a British journalist specializing in the Horn of Africa, noted that the US needs Eritrea in the struggle to secure the Red Sea against the Houthis, an Iran-backed Shiite Muslim militia.
Plaut argues that removing sanctions gives new political weight to one of Africa's most repressive regimes.

As fighting resumes in Tigray, Eritrea could once again become a decisive military player. Plaut said that the current tensions had the potential of developing into a broader regional confrontation, which, he said, "is the most serious danger."

In his view, US President Donald Trump's administration has already made a strategic calculation: "Trump has now mended fences with Eritrea and has lifted sanctions against Eritrea" in an effort to reduce the threat posed by the Houthis and secure the Red Sea.

blocks.caption: Eritrea's location at the Bab Al-Mandab Strait is an asset for the autocratic nation, as partners from near and far seek access to the Red SeaImage: ABACA/picture alliance

blocks.text: A striking coincidence of timing
The escalation in Tigray came only days after Washington removed key Eritrean entities and individuals from its sanctions list.

On September 18, the United States allowed the national emergency underpinning its Ethiopia-related sanctions regime to expire. The Treasury Department subsequently removed a number of Eritrean individuals and entities from its sanctions list, including senior financial official Hagos Ghebrehiwet and the Red Sea Trading Corporation. The measures had originally been imposed in 2021 in connection with the Tigray war.

US officials have not described the move as an endorsement of Eritrea, nor has Washington publicly said that it struck a deal with Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki. But it removes a layer of pressure on a government whose strategic importance has grown as security around the Red Sea deteriorates.
For Abdurahman Sayed, director of the Horn of Africa Centre for Regional Integration and a political analyst, the wider geopolitical context is crucial.

"It is happening at a time when the war on Iran is ongoing," he told DW. "The Strait of Hormuz has been blocked for some time, and now the Bab el-Mendeb on the Red Sea, where Eritrea is located, this may give Eritrea some advantage to establish a meaningful relationship with the US."
Why Eritrea matters
Eritrea controls a long coastline opposite Yemen. Its southern port of Assab lies close to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, one of the world's most important maritime chokepoints.
Moses Okello, a senior researcher at the Institute for Security Studies in Addis Ababa, says the regional context has fundamentally changed since the previous Tigray war.

"In 2020, the concern was the TPLF [Tigray People's Liberation Front] versus the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF)," he told DW. "Today, the entire Middle East is up in flames, and now the tensions in the Red Sea. So this changes the strategic value of not just the Eritrean coast, but the entire Red Sea waterway."
Why northern Ethiopia is seeing growing violence once again
For Washington, cooperation — or at least non-hostility — from Eritrea can therefore be strategically valuable.
But the bargain carries risks.

Eritrea is one of the world's most authoritarian states, with no national elections since independence in 1993 and an extensive system of indefinite national service. Eritrean forces also fought alongside Ethiopian federal troops during the 2020-22 Tigray war.

And the economic impact of lifting sanctions may be more limited than the political symbolism suggests. "Lifting the sanctions may not make a huge difference on the ground," said Sayed. "Eritrea is not a trade hub [nor does it have] a well-established trading relationship with the outside world. It's actually a closed country."
Ethiopia heads back towards war
The latest fighting did not emerge from nowhere.

On September 21, seven Ethiopian armed and political groups announced an alliance aimed at removing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government. The coalition includes the TPLF, the Amhara Fano National Movement and the Oromo Liberation Army. Some members were on opposing sides during the 2020-22 Tigray war.
It remains unclear how closely the alliance's members will coordinate militarily. The alliance brings together groups with very different histories that share opposition to the federal government.

Two days later, fighting escalated in Tigray. Tigrayan forces seized airports and fighting spread into neighboring regions. The TPLF says federal forces attacked first; Addis Ababa says the TPLF launched the offensive.
The renewed fighting has raised questions about the durability of the 2022 Pretoria agreement.
Could Eritrea intervene?
During the previous Tigray war, Eritrean forces fought alongside Ethiopian federal troops. But relations between Afwerki and Abiy have since deteriorated sharply.

One major dispute concerns Ethiopia's demand for reliable access to the Red Sea. Landlocked since Eritrea's independence, Ethiopia regards maritime access as a strategic necessity. Eritrea insists on its sovereignty and has rejected any suggestion that Ethiopia could obtain access through coercion.
The new rebel alliance transforming the Tigray conflict
The Ethiopian government has accused Eritrea of supporting armed groups in the new conflict. Eritrea denies such allegations.

There is currently no public evidence that the US sanctions decision was designed to encourage Eritrean military intervention in Ethiopia. Nor is it clear that Asmara has decided to enter the fighting.
But if the Tigray conflict intensifies, Eritrea could see a direct security interest in intervening. That would transform an Ethiopian conflict into a potentially interstate confrontation.
A regional conflict waiting to spread
The Horn of Africa is already exceptionally volatile.

Sudan remains at war. Somalia is unstable. Ethiopia and Egypt remain locked in a dispute over the Nile and the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam. Saudi Arabia and the UAE are pursuing their own interests across the Red Sea and Horn of Africa. And the conflict in Yemen is directly connected to the security of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

Okello sees the changing Middle East as an additional reason for urgent engagement. "There is no doubt that the conflict in the Middle East now puts a new contextual layer over that primary tension and increases the urgency to engage with both Eritrea and Addis Ababa to try and address this before it becomes a conflagration which makes addressing issues in the Red Sea a lot more difficult."
A new Ethiopia-Eritrea confrontation would therefore not happen in isolation.

Plaut warns that regional alliances could interact in dangerous ways. "You have the UAE backing the RSF and you have the Saudis backing the Eritreans and the Sudanese Armed Forces," he told DW. "This could all multiply and you could get one conflict leading into another."

That does not mean a general regional war is inevitable. Most governments involved have strong reasons to prevent an uncontrollable escalation. But the number of links between the region's conflicts is increasing.
Eritrea and shifting regional dynamics
For Eritrea's President Afwerki, the US decision is an opportunity.

The end of the sanctions removes one source of international pressure and may give Eritrea greater diplomatic room for maneuver. More importantly, Washington's renewed engagement with Asmara underscores the strategic value of Eritrea's Red Sea position.
Why can't Ethiopia and Eritrea be friends?

The more important Eritrea becomes to US and regional security calculations, the greater the danger that strategic interests will overshadow concerns about its authoritarian system and past military interventions.
For Ethiopia, the immediate question is whether the renewed fighting can be stopped before it draws in Eritrea.
For Washington, the challenge is whether Eritrea can be engaged as a Red Sea security partner without giving Asmara greater freedom to destabilize its neighbors.
Eritrea has spent decades on the margins of international diplomacy. Its location on the Red Sea has long given it strategic significance.

With fighting again raging in Tigray, the Houthis threatening the Red Sea and Washington reopening its channel to Asmara, Eritrea could become one of the key players in the Horn of Africa's next chapter.
Ekinder Firew in Addis Ababa contributed to this report.

articles.title: Social media franchising? Palace says further study needed
articles.summary: In connection with recent school shootings that are believed to have been caused by online influences, Palace saw merit in the proposed measure to require social media platforms to be licensed before…

blocks.text: Published September 25, 2026 9:30pm

In connection with recent school shootings that are believed to have been caused by online influences, Palace saw merit in the proposed measure to require social media platforms to be licensed before they could operate in the Philippines but maintained that further studies are required.

In a press briefing in Ilocos Norte, Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said that President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. found it hard to understand how the South Cotabato school shooter could open fire on his schoolmates.
The Banga National High School shooting led to three deaths—including the shooter himself.
Asked about a House Bill No. 4786 or a proposed measure mandating social media platforms to have a legislative franchise, Castro said that the measure needed further review.

“Sa panukalang iyan patungkol sa pagpapalagay o kinakailangan ng prangkisa ng mga social media platforms, magandang panukala pero dapat aralin kung ano ang maaaring maidulot nito – maaaring may positibo, maaaring may negatibo, maaaring may maaapektuhang mga negosyo, maaaring may maapektuhan ibang mga tao na gumagamit ng mga social media platforms na ito,” Castro said.

(That measure that mandates a franchise for social media platforms, it is a good measure but it needs to be studied because of what it could entail — it could be positive, it could be negative, there could be businesses affected, there could be some social media users who are affected.)
Castro said this after the Department of Information and Communications Technology’s (DICT) Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) garnered criticism for banning Discord.
The CICC had issued an ultimatum to the social media platform, compelling it to designate a country representative,
While she did not address the matter directly, Castro issued a warning against social media platforms that do not collaborate with the government.

“Kailangan na ring gamitin ang ‘strong political will’ ng Pangulo sa mga maaaring pasaway na social media platforms na hindi tumutulong sa pamahalaan para sugpuin ang ganitong karahasan,” Castro said.
(The President must use his ‘strong political will’ against possibly errant social media platforms that do not help the government to stop these types of violence.) –NB, GMA News

articles.title: Comelec orders cessation of activities for 2026 barangay and SK elections
articles.summary: The Commission on Elections (Comelec) on Friday ordered the cessation of all activities related to the 2026 Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections (BSKE).

blocks.text: Published September 25, 2026 9:25pm
The Commission on Elections (Comelec) on Friday ordered the cessation of all activities related to the 2026 Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections (BSKE).
This is after President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. signed into law a bill postponing the BSKE, previously scheduled for November 2, 2026.
Based on its latest resolution, Comelec said among the activities ordered stopped are the filing of certificates of candidacy and the subsequent campaign period.

COMELEC also ordered the lifting of prohibitions on certain acts in connection to the conduct of the elections under the previously approved calendar of activities and related laws, rules, and regulations.
However, the poll body said some preparations will continue.

The ongoing printing of additional ballots, accountable forms, Election Day Computerized Voters List (EDCVL), and Posted Computerized Voters List (PCVL) will continue until the allocated quantities are completed.
Pending procurement of BSKE-related forms and supplies will also be completed, including their delivery.
All election forms, supplies, and other paraphernalia already printed or procured for the 2026 BSKE should be secured, properly stored, and preserved for future use, according to the poll body.
Voter registration for the 2028 National and Local Elections will continue, starting in the second week of November 2026. –NB, GMA News
