articles.title: Man shot during 2024 Trump campaign rally in Butler dies
articles.summary: A gunman shot Jim Copenhaver twice while also killing another man and grazing Trump's ear with a bullet.

blocks.text: In a post on his social media site Truth Social, Trump called Copenhaver a "true American patriot".

"More than two years ago in Butler, Pennsylvania, a crazed gunman attempted to stifle our America First Movement. Instead, Jim and so many other wonderful Patriots who love our Country, stood united in defense of our shared values of Freedom, Liberty, and Justice," Trump said. "Our hearts and prayers are with the Copenhaver family, especially his incredible wife Marianne."
An attorney for Copenhaver's family said his dedication to the US was a "defining part of his life".
"As a veteran, he proudly served our nation in the armed forces, and his love of country never wavered," the lawyer said in a statement to the BBC's US partner CBS News.
In an interview with CBS a year after the Butler rally, Copenhaver and David Dutch, the third attendee who was shot, said they had been through infections and surgeries after being wounded.
Copenhaver was shot in the arm and the abdomen. A year later, the bullet was still lodged in his body next to his spine, he told CBS, causing him to walk with a cane.
Both Dutch and Copenhaver sued the federal government for damages in June, arguing the Secret Service failed to ensure their safety and was therefore liable for their injuries.
Republicans in the US House of Representatives also paid tribute to Copenhaver on Friday, saying in a social media post: "Jim endured unimaginable hardship with strength and perseverance."

articles.title: Mother recalls killings of 4 sons in Davao before Truth Commission
articles.summary: A 72-year-old mother whose four sons were killed in Davao City testified before the Truth Commission on extrajudicial killings on Friday, recounting alleged threats against her children and her…

blocks.text: Published September 25, 2026 9:22pm

A 72-year-old mother whose four sons were killed in Davao City testified before the Truth Commission on extrajudicial killings on Friday, recounting alleged threats against her children and her decades-long search for justice.
"Kung totoo man na ganoon ang mga anak ko, dapat pinapreso sila, hindi papatayin," Nanay Alia said as translated by an interpreter during the Commission's hearing.
(If the accusations against my children were true, they should have been imprisoned, not killed.)
Nanay Alia said she had been seeking justice for about 25 years for her sons Richard, Christopher, Bobby and Fernando, who were killed when they were still teenagers.
In July 2001, Alia found 18-year-old Richard dead with stab wounds. She said she later learned that Richard had allegedly been threatened by police before his death.
“Sabi ng pulis, isa-isahin niya ang mga anak ko,” Nanay Alia said.
(The police said he would kill my children one by one.)

Christopher was 18 when he was killed in October 2001 also from stab wounds. After a year, Bobby, 14 years old, was killed after his arrest in November 2002. He was later found severely beaten and stabbed. Fernando, 15 years old, was also stabbed and died in April 2007.
Nanay Alia said she believed the Davao Death Squad existed based on what she said she experienced and learned about the deaths of her children.
“Merong mga nagsasabi na hindi naman daw totoo itong mga DDS, yung Davao Death Squad. Hindi, totoo yan. Kasi kilala ko ‘yan sila. Alam ko yung sistema nila,” she said.
(There are those who say that these DDS, the Davao Death Squad, are not real. No, they are real. Because I know them. I know their operation.)

“Isa lang yung nakita ko sa kanila, yung mga anak ko. Yung pagpatay kay Topher o kay Bobby. Yung pumatay sa kanya, dating preso. Ito kasing DDS, isang grupo ng mga pulis na malalaki, matataas ang ranggo. Tapos kukuha sila ng ibang tao. Sila ang papatay. Para sila mismo, safe lang,” she added.

(I only saw one of them, in the case of my children. The killing of Topher or Bobby. The one who killed him was a former prisoner. This is the DDS, a group of big, high-ranking police officers. Then they will hire other people. They will kill. So that they themselves are safe.)
Forensic pathologist Dr. Raquel Fortun said the killings of Alia’s children should have been thoroughly investigated.
Fortun said Christopher had multiple stab wounds to the chest, including injuries affecting the heart and lungs, and a cut on his forearm that could be considered a defensive wound.
“Ibig sabihin, nakapag-react siya noong siya ay inatake. Ito yung tinatawag nating defensive wound,” she said.
(This means he was able to react when he was attacked. This is what we call a defensive wound.)
Richard had facial injuries and a stab wound to the chest that allegedly affected his lung and caused internal bleeding.
Both bodies had reportedly been embalmed before examination.
The records reviewed appeared to have been prepared by one doctor and the reports contained limited information, according to Fortun.
She said the Commission would seek additional records, including the death certificates of Bobby and Fernando, possible autopsy records, and hospital records concerning Fernando.
Fortun said the similar use of sharp force injuries in the four deaths raised questions about whether the killings involved the same assailant or group.

The Truth Commission was organized as an independent, civil society-led body tasked to find out the truth about "drug war" killings in the Philippines, restore dignity to the victims, and foster healing and reform.—LDF, GMA News

articles.title: A HRW report shows how South Korean women face systemic barriers to climbing the career ladder
articles.summary: A new report shows how in South Korea, women on average earn less and have fewer employment opportunities throughout their lives.

image.caption: Career interruptions, occupational segregation and discrimination within organizations, drive South Korea's gender gap [FILE August 2021]Image: DW

blocks.text: At 27, a woman in South Korea earns 8% less than male peers. By her late 50s, she earns 50% less. This is according to government wage data published in a recent Human Rights Watch (HRW) report.

South Korea is a global technology and industrial powerhouse, but its gender pay gap has remained the highest in the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) since comparable records began in 1992.
"The gender division of labor inside the home leads directly to a gender division of labor in the labor market," Min Hee Kim, a Korean activist for women labor struggles, told DW.

The problem, she argues, is not simply that women are paid less than men. As women age, the kinds of work available to them narrows and the consequences of lower pay, career breaks and precarious jobs accumulate.
For the report, "Too Old and a Woman," HRW interviewed 41 South Korean women aged 28 to 87 about their working lives.
Structural barriers to women's careers

Discrimination has changed form rather than disappeared, Kim said. Until the 1980s, it was legal for employers to fire women simply for getting married, a practice known as "marriage-based dismissal," where employers assumed a married woman would soon leave to raise children anyway.

Today, "it is difficult to openly say, 'We won't hire you because you're a woman,'" Kim added. But caregiving responsibilities still fall on women, pushing them into lower-paid jobs when they try to return to work.
According to the HRW report, women's university attainment has passed men's since the 1980s. Higher education would suggest equal opportunity after graduation, but the job market says otherwise.
One year after graduating, women already earn 22% less than men, according to a 2024 study.
Many women told HRW that after leaving work for marriage or children, chances of returning to the workforce were limited to a handful of jobs such as call centers, cleaning or caregiving.
Women who opt to focus on their career told HRW they hit a glass ceiling at work. Women held 18% of manager jobs in 2024, and only five of 38 senior civil servants were women.
Brains, beauty and barriers: the global job market
Wages peak and drop off
Women's wages peak in their late 30s and then steadily decline, according to Labor Ministry survey data cited by HRW.
South Korea's Gender Ministry told HRW that career interruptions, along with occupational segregation and discrimination within organizations, drive the gap.
J. Mi-sook, 53, told HRW that her three years of experience weren't recognized by her next employer, so she started at entry level on a lower salary.
The longer women spend outside the workforce, the less experience they accumulate on their resumes, which results in less pay and less work stability.

Kim pointed to structural discrimination, a concept from the report that HRW describes as discrimination so embedded in social practices and institutions that even the people harmed by it may not recognize it as a problem.

"When you are alone, it is easy to think, 'It's because I'm not capable enough,' or 'It's because I'm getting older,'" she said. It's only when women who've had similar experiences meet and talk, she added, that they realize, "this wasn't just my problem."
It gets harder as you get older

Park Jae-soon, 61, was forced to retire at 60 from a utility company and now works part-time as a care worker. Her annual income fell from 55 million won ($40,500/€35,600) to 15.6 million won, a 72% drop.
HRW argues the mandatory retirement age and the "peak wage" system, which lets employers cut older workers' pay in the years before retirement, should both be abolished.
According to data cited in the report, women received 53% of men's National Old Age Pension on average in October 2025, a 47% gap.
"I think what is important here is that this is not simply a problem of middle-aged women having difficulty finding jobs," Kim said.

"The work that women have traditionally done inside the home, like cleaning, cooking, caregiving and managing other people's emotions, is classified as 'work suitable for women' when it enters the labor market, and then low wages are assigned to it," she added.
How South Korea's cosmetic industry drives career success
From first paycheck to pension
HRW argues the disadvantage builds stage by stage, from a woman's first paycheck up until her pension.

"Career interruption among women in their 30s is already a pension issue," Kim said. "Part-time work among women in their 40s is a pension issue, and low wages among women in their 50s are already a pension issue," she added.
South Korea's government has said it will pursue a phased increase in the statutory retirement age from 60 to 65.

"This cannot be solved with just one policy. Equal pay for equal work needs to be actually implemented, wage structures need to be transparent, and care needs to be treated as a public responsibility rather than something that is pushed onto individual families and women," Kim said.
The rights activist said the report is an important starting point, but believes its picture is incomplete.

Most interviewees were recruited through civic organizations and largely in Seoul, she noted, while disabled women, migrant workers and others may experience a different combination of age and gender discrimination.

"The important question is not simply, 'How much discrimination do women face?'" she said. "It is which women, in what positions, become increasingly distanced from which resources and rights as they grow older."

articles.title: DPWH projects flagged by Gatchalian in 2027 proposed budget
articles.summary: Senator Win Gatchalian spots projects without station limits or bridge IDs, duplicated projects, and projects without coordinates in the proposed 2027 budget of the Department of Public Works and…

blocks.text: Senator Win Gatchalian spots projects without station limits or bridge IDs, duplicated projects, and projects without coordinates in the proposed 2027 budget of the Department of Public Works and Highways
MANILA, Philippines – Senator Win Gatchalian flagged 7,107 projects worth P251.81 billion in the proposed 2027 budget of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH).
Among the red flags Gatchalian raised during the Senate budget hearing on Friday, September 25, were:

items: Projects without station limits or bridge IDs: P83.67 billion for 2,570 projects
Duplicated projects: P3.94 billion for 189 projects
Projects reappearing from the 2026 General Appropriations Act in the 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP): P20.79 billion for 258 projects
Projects without coordinates: P83.50 billion for 3,543 projects
Lump-sum projects: P14.79 billion for 56 projects
Overlapping or fragmented projects: P63.19 billion for 533 projects
Unspecified work scope: P1.52 billion for 62 projects
Conflicting types of work: P386.25 million for 20 projects

blocks.text: Given the sheer volume of projects handled by the agency, DPWH Secretary Vince Dizon said they presume regularity in the proposals submitted by regional and district offices.
Dizon said the DPWH would review the projects flagged by Gatchalian. He also pointed out that the projects included in the NEP came with a certificate of implementability.
The document, signed by a district engineer, certifies that a proposed project has no duplicate, has not received previous funding, and does not overlap with another project.
If the review finds problems with the flagged projects, Dizon said the DPWH would file cases against the concerned district engineers.
At the same time, Dizon acknowledged that some of the projects flagged by Gatchalian could be explained.
Gatchalian also flagged multi-billion-peso projects in the 2026 budget proposal.
In 2025, it was revealed that DPWH officials had connived with contractors and lawmakers to corrupt public funds. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Eldrew Yulo continues to prove boundless potential with Asian Games bronze
articles.summary: After his older brother Carlos captured back-to-back golds in floor exercise and vault, Eldrew Yulo also shines in his first Asian Games stint as he bags the bronze in horizontal bar

blocks.text: SWING. Eldrew Yulo in action for the Philippines in the 2026 Asian Games.
PSC-POC Media Pool
After his older brother Carlos captured back-to-back golds in floor exercise and vault, Eldrew Yulo also shines in his first Asian Games stint as he bags the bronze in horizontal bar
MANILA, Philippines – Winning is a family affair for Eldrew and Carlos Yulo.

After his older brother Carlos captured back-to-back artistic gymnastics golds in floor exercise and vault, Eldrew also shone in the 2026 Asian Games as he bagged the bronze in horizontal bar at the Nagoya General Gymnasium in Japan on Friday, September 25.
The younger Yulo completed the podium after a tiebreaker with Kazakhstan’s Milad Karimi, scoring 13.666 points to conclude his first Asian Games stint in style.

blocks.caption: EMOTIONS. The Philippines’ Karl Jahrel Eldrew Yulo bursts into tears after winning the bronze medal in the men’s horizontal bar in the artistic gymnastics competition of the 2026 Asian Games.

blocks.text: Yulo and Karimi posted similar scores, but the Filipino clinched the bronze with a higher execution of 8.566 against the 7.766 of the veteran Kazakh, who is a former Asian champion in the apparatus.
Tian Hao won convincingly with 14.7 points as he secured another gold medal for China, which dominated the competition and ruled five of the eight events in men’s artistic gymnastics.
Japan’s Shinnosuke Oka settled for silver anew with 14.033 points — the gold once again eluding him following runner-up finishes in the team, individual all-around, and parallel bars.
The Asian Games medal is yet another testament to the boundless potential of Yulo, who just turned 18 in January and is competing in his first year as a senior gymnast.
And his rookie year has been fruitful.

Yulo won gold and bronze medals in floor exercise and a bronze in horizontal bar in the FIG World Cup Series as well as a floor exercise bronze in the Asian Artistic Gymnastics Championships in China in June.
If the Asian Games is any indication, Yulo is just getting started. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Mary Jane Veloso finally free after 16 years
articles.summary: Veloso, who was sentenced to death in Indonesia in 2010 for drug trafficking, is given absolute pardon by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

blocks.text: REPATRIATION. Mary Jane Veloso gestures during a press conference, prior to her repatriation to the Philippines, at the Soekarno-Hatta International Airport in Jakarta, Indonesia, December 17, 2024.
Ajeng Dinar Ulfiana/Reuters
Veloso, who was sentenced to death in Indonesia in 2010 for drug trafficking, is given absolute pardon by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

items: Mary Jane Veloso, a former overseas Filipino worker and human trafficking victim, was released from detention after more than a decade following an absolute pardon granted by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
Veloso was sentenced to death in Indonesia in 2010 for drug trafficking, claiming she was tricked by her recruiters into carrying heroin unknowingly.
Her release comes after an agreement between the Philippine and Indonesian governments, with her recruiters currently detained for illegal recruitment.

MANILA, Philippines – After more than a decade in detention, Mary Jane Veloso, the woman who suffered in jail after she was allegedly tricked by recruiters into becoming a drug mule, is finally walking free.
The former overseas Filipino worker and human trafficking victim was released from the Correctional Institution for Women (CIW) in Mandaluyong City on Friday night, September 25.
This comes a day after President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. granted her absolute pardon on Thursday, September 24.
Bureau of Corrections Director General Gregorio Catapang Jr. handed Mary Jane Veloso a copy of the President’s absolute pardon and presented her official release order from the CIW on Friday night.

In a statement, the bureau said Veloso will be endorsed to the local government unit of her residence in Nueva Ecija “as part of the government’s reintegration,” which includes “access [to] programs and services designed to support her transition back into the community.”
“This only proves that there are really second chances, and we are happy that Veloso can now enjoy her newfound freedom with her family,” Catapang said.

blocks.caption: Marcos pardons Mary Jane Veloso

blocks.text: Veloso, who was sentenced to death in Indonesia in 2010 for drug trafficking, was given an absolute pardon by the President. This extinguished her criminal liability.
In 2010, Veloso was supposed to fly to Malaysia to work as an overseas Filipino worker, but was instead rerouted to Yogyakarta, Indonesia, where her recruiters gave her a new suitcase.

Indonesian authorities found that the bag contained a stash of heroin, which Veloso claimed she unknowingly brought with her. Even after she was sentenced to death due to drug trafficking, Veloso and her lawyers from the National Union of People’s Lawyers maintained that she was innocent and was only allegedly tricked by her recruiters into being their drug mule.

Veloso was scheduled for execution in 2015, but then-president Benigno Aquino III broke protocol at the last minute and called then-Indonesian foreign minister Retno Marsudi to turn Veloso into a state witness. (LOOK BACK: Aquino, Del Rosario, and the phone call that saved Mary Jane Veloso’s life)

In 2024, Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto entered into an agreement with the Philippine government to transfer Veloso to the country. Indonesia also gave Marcos the discretion to grant Veloso clemency.
She arrived in the Philippines in December 2024 and had been detained at CIW since then.

Veloso’s recruiter Cristina Sergio and accomplice Julius Lacanilao are currently detained after they were found guilty of illegal recruitment in 2020. In June, Veloso took the witness stand and personally testified in the human trafficking and illegal recruitment case against her recruiters. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Pomp over progress as Trump rolls out red carpet for China’s president Xi Jinping
articles.summary: While the US president hailed the visit as ‘great’, almost nothing of substance was achieved, which was a win for Xi

blocks.text: If the Beijing meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in May was the “stalemate summit”, the second round of talks between the presidents of the US and China this week seemed to give up entirely on the idea of breakthroughs.

Instead, it was dubbed a celebration of “diplotainment” rather than diplomacy, where pomp prevailed over progress, and where one of the main outcomes was the news that two giant pandas would soon be sent from China to the Atlanta Zoo.

Trump rolled out the red carpet for Xi when he landed on Wednesday, and broke with decades of precedent to meet the Chinese leader at Joint Base Andrews. Thus began a three-day state visit which involved a tour of Trump’s new helipad, the Marine One helicopter, and a 90-minute meeting which Trump described as “great” and which revealed, according to Trump, that Xi “has great interest in granite”.
“The biggest takeaways is that Trump has been displaying an extraordinary degree of deference to Xi Jinping,” said Julian Gewirtz, who served as a senior China official in the Biden administration.
But what of actual substance? Expectations going into the summit were low. But the outcomes somehow still fell short.

blocks.caption: Expectations going into the summit were low. Photograph: Saul Loeb/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: One of the biggest issues in the US-China relationship is trade. Last year, as Trump unveiled successive rounds of tariffs on Chinese goods, the White House accused China of unfair practices that contributed to the loss of 3.7m US jobs and inflated the trade deficit. The tariffs were supposed to suppress the volume of Chinese imports to the US and put pressure on China.

To some degree, they worked. The US trade deficit with China in 2025 fell to $200bn, down from nearly $300bn in 2024. But experts have noted that some of this shortfall is made up for by Chinese goods being shipped to the US via third countries, a trend underlined by the fact that China’s trade surplus surpassed a record $1tn last year.

With the US and China accounting for 43% of global GDP, their trade war has far-reaching implications for the world economy. So it was a relief not just to Beijing and to US consumers when the two countries agreed a temporary truce in Busan last year.

That truce is due to expire in November. China, where the economy is heavily reliant on exports, was reported to be pushing for the truce to be extended until the end of Trump’s term, in January 2029.

On Thursday, it was revealed that Xi’s first state visit to the US in over a decade had resulted in a mere two-month extension. That reflects “the lack of preparation for this summit beyond the pomp and circumstance,” said Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society.

“This summit largely achieved symbolism and ritualism over substance. That is very clear,” said William Yang, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group. The short extension “reflects the level of fundamental differences that still exist between the two countries over a variety of issues.”

China’s most powerful response to Trump’s tariffs was the decision to block the export of rare earths, critical minerals vital to US manufacturing and military supply chains. That seemed to skewer Trump’s leverage over China.
“Beijing’s retaliation … seems to have had a profound effect on [Trump] and his administration’s willingness to take risks vis a vis China,” said Gewirtz.

Apart from the trade war agreement, the summit failed to achieve any meaningful progress on thorny issues in the US-China relationship such as artificial intelligence, Taiwan, the wars in Iran and Ukraine, and human rights.

blocks.caption: For China, the lack of big news from the state visit is a win in itself. Photograph: Annabelle Gordon/EPA

blocks.text: On Taiwan, which Beijing considers to be the most important issue in the relationship, Xi put pressure on Trump to weaken the US’s support for the self-governing island that China claims as its own. According to the Chinese readout of the X-Trump meeting, Xi told Trump that he hoped “the US side will adhere to the correct position of opposing Taiwan independence”.

For the US to state that it “opposes” Taiwanese independence would be a rhetorical shift from the current position of “does not support” such a claim, and would be a move welcomed by Beijing. Trump has not yet commented on whether he agreed to such a statement. But it does seem he is no closer to approving a $14bn arms sale package for Taiwan, a sale which Beijing would like to see disappear completely.

On Thursday, US Senate Democrats lambasted Trump for opting for “pageantry over purpose” and for failing to deliver agreements on “the economic and security issues that will shape America’s future”. Trump ignored recent warnings about the dangers posed by AI, writing on social media on Thursday: “I want ​to leave it exactly where it is”, adding: “That is China’s position also.”

For China, the lack of big news from the visit is a win in itself. “The summit went excellently from the Chinese perspective,” said Thomas. Xi “got a huge amount of respect from the American president, the full state visit treatment [and] really great images beaming back to China of the Chinese and the American presidents interacting as peers on the global stage without having to make any meaningful concessions or compromises.”

articles.title: Internet restricted after fighting breaks out in Ethiopia's Tigray region
articles.summary: During the two-year civil war in Tigray, the region was totally cut off from the outside world.

blocks.text: Internet and call services have been disrupted in Ethiopia's northern region of Tigray after fighting broke out this week between regional forces and the national army.

Services provided by state-owned telecoms operator Ethio Telecom have been completely cut, although those from the much smaller private firm Safaricom remain operational. Internet monitoring group NetBlocks earlier posted on X that network data indicated a sub-national internet shutdown in northern Tigray.
"Last night telecommunications got knocked out," Duke Burbridge, an American humanitarian worker in Tigray's capital, Mekelle, told the BBC's Newsday programme.
The BBC has contacted Ethiopia's authorities for comment.
Burbridge said there had been a scarcity of cash in Tigray for the past eight months, with people unable to access ATMs so the lack of internet services would be "devastating for everybody".
Many people rely on banking and mobile money applications for transactions, with the majority using Ethio Telecom and Safaricom's networks to access these services.
Clashes between Tigrayan forces and their allies and Ethiopia's federal troops broke out on Wednesday, prompting heightened tension and reports of panic buying.
During the two-year civil which ended in 2022, Tigray was totally cut off from the outside world.
Limited access to cash, food and medicine pushed hundreds of thousands into famine-like conditions.
Additional reporting by Peter Mwai, BBC Verify

articles.title: Robin Padilla's counter-affidavit filing reset to Nov. 12, 2026
articles.summary: Senator Robin Padilla was not able to file his counter-affidavit at the Department of Justice (DOJ) on Friday due to the lack of documents.

blocks.text: Published September 25, 2026 8:31pm
Senator Robin Padilla was not able to file his counter-affidavit at the Department of Justice (DOJ) on Friday due to the lack of documents.
Padilla’s submission of his counter-affidavit is now set for November 12, so that he can also swear to it.

In a DZBB report from Tuesday Niu, the DOJ had wrapped up the first day of its preliminary investigation into the obstruction of justice charges filed against Padilla for allegedly aiding the escape of Sen. Bato dela Rosa.

However, Padilla was unable to file his counter-affidavit. The Panel of Prosecutors noted that the Philippine National Police Criminal Investigation and Detection Group (PNP CIDG) lacked a few documents.
As a result, the Panel of Prosecutors asked the PNP CIDG for additional requirements.
The next preliminary investigation is on October 9, but Padilla will no longer attend, opting to have his lawyers represent him.
Lawyer Jimmy Bondoc also arrived with Padilla at the DOJ; however, he said that he was representing another client in the same case. He did not disclose who his client was for privacy reasons.
Outside of the DOJ, Padilla’s supporters held a demonstration. The senator spoke to them directly and thanked them. Sen. Bong Go was also at the DOJ to show his support for Padilla.
Authorities attempted to issue Dela Rosa an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court for alleged crimes against humanity.

Dela Rosa fled the Senate premises in the early morning of May 14, hours after a shooting incident took place in the Upper Chamber. Padilla has previously admitted to allowing Dela Rosa to hitch a ride in his car after the incident. —Jean Mangaluz/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: As wildfire season winds down, people in B.C. communities are rebuilding their lives
articles.summary: As wildfire season winds down, British Columbia communities affected are now shifting to recovery efforts, while those who lost home sift through ashes and attempt to rebuild their lives.

image.caption: Joel Patan stands outside the remains of his home that was destroyed by the Bald Range wildfire near Faulder, west of Summerland, B.C., on Sept. 18. He is among hundreds of people that are having to pick up the pieces after this summer's devastating fire season. (Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Joel Patan says his "life is ashes" now, as he sifts through the ruins of his home that was incinerated last month, along with most structures in the small community of Faulder outside Summerland, B.C.
"It's just gut-wrenching," he said.
Patan, who runs an HVAC company, said his family moved onto their "dream property" in December 2024, buying it after flipping two other homes.

He said there were once more than 80 homes in Faulder, but most were destroyed by the Bald Range wildfire that roared eastward on the evening of Aug. 7, setting off an evacuation of thousands from Okanagan communities.
An 80-year-old woman who lived in Meadow Valley nearby died suddenly during the evacuation, and Penticton RCMP said it was believed her death was "a result of the wildfire."
"Running from a fire, grabbing everything you have, like I don't think people understand. When we talk about 'We ran from a fire,' we ran," Patan said.
"I had RCMP yelling at me, 'Get out of your house,' after I found the cat finally, [they were] basically saying, 'The flames are right there.'"
B.C. RCMP investigating cause of explosive Bald Range wildfire
The Bald Range fire is still burning but is listed as under control by the B.C. Wildfire Service. Wildfire activity is dying down as summer weather gives way to fall.
And families like Patan's now face the prospect of rebuilding and recovering from the devastation of losing the roof over their heads.
The wildfire season in B.C. has burned far less area than usual, just 1,350 square kilometres, only about a quarter of the 20-year average.
But it has been one of the most devastating seasons on record for property destruction, with more than 500 homes or other structures destroyed or damaged.
About 150 of those were lost to the Bald Range fire, including 110 in Faulder and Meadow Valley, and 40 in the nearby Okanagan lakeside community of Summerland.

On the northern shores of Okanagan Lake, the Bradley Complex of fires near Vernon brought ruin right to the waterline, some residents watching from boats as their homes burned in early August. Some 230 homes on the lands of the Okanagan Indian Band were lost.
About 240 kilometres to the northwest, the Big Bar Complex of fires destroyed structures on around 120 properties outside Clinton, B.C.
Meanwhile, the Brunswick Complex of fires outside Boston Bar in the Fraser Canyon, 200 kilometres northeast of Vancouver, damaged seven structures, four of them homes or cabins.
No single path to recovery
There is no singular path to recovery, either on an individual or community level.

The Ministry of Emergency Management and Climate Readiness said in a statement that "recovery looks different for each community and is led by local governments and First Nations with support from the province, federal partners, non-government organizations, businesses and community members."

It said it has assigned "community recovery officers" to work with impacted areas and will "continue supporting local governments and First Nations as they lead recovery efforts in their communities, including through recovery planning, governance, co-ordination and available supports."
Access to Faulder is still restricted, with a checkpoint allowing people in only if they have a permit. Private security guards roam the community to protect against looting.

Blackened trees line Princeton-Summerland Road to Faulder, where homes have been reduced to their foundations, with burnt shells of vehicles a common sight along the winding road into the hills above the valley.
Patan said he's now dealing with his insurer, considering himself lucky since many Faulder residents were either uninsured or underinsured and are now focused on survival.
The cleanup of damaged properties, he said, also has to factor in other potential hazards, including silica dust, asbestos and other potential contaminants like lead and mercury.

"People are trying to bring their trailers in with no water and that's another scary thing. They're bringing in trailers. Some people don't have electrical. We don't an adequate source of water right now … but people need somewhere to live."
The smell of the fire still hangs in the air around the charred foundation of Patan's home. Broken glass and other debris crunches and cracks under his feet as he surveys the ruin.
Patan descends the stairs into what used to be his basement, pointing out one of his daughter's porcelain dolls' heads in the rubble.
"You're standing in what above me was my master bedroom," he said, his arms outstretched to the sky.
Exactly how far his insurance will go is an open question, but he laments all that was lost in the evacuation, including one of his daughter's first pair of shoes.
Battling Summerland blaze 'like a jet engine coming up behind you': firefighter
Soft-spoken Patan said even though there have been tears and grief, he's optimistic, something he says is a childhood trait.
"My mom and dad would tell you, when I had a bad day, I would wake up the next day like it never happened," he said.

"We'll build a house that is good for wildfire interface, good for our family, still the same four bedrooms, three baths, things that we may have not liked about our house, we'll repair, we may fix — but again, we have to see within the confines of our insurance, but whatever we can do to get back what we had, and then it's just a new beginning, and we just move forward."
"I will buy my daughters every toy they want," he added.
Trying to ease burden of recovery

Erick Thompson, senior manager of communications and engagement with the Regional District of Okanagan Similkameen, said the focus is both on recovery and "providing support to those people who have lost property, lost a home, lost outbuildings."

"Recovery is a long phase and there's a lot that goes along with that," he said. "Remediation of properties, removal of debris, so the RDOS is helping with other agencies to co-ordinate a lot of that.
"But in the aftermath of this wildfire, recovery is always a challenge and when people have lost a home, especially if they're not insured, the local government's role is to advocate for them."

He said the Union of British Columbia Municipalities convention in Vancouver last week saw regional district staff advocating for things like waiving provincial sales tax for people trying to rebuild and help with debris removal.

The regional district said in a statement on Monday that officials at the convention "emphasized the need for measures that help reduce the financial burden on residents rebuilding homes, properties, and livelihoods."
Relief from provincial sales tax, it said, is "a critical area for provincial consideration."

"Many residents are facing substantial rebuilding costs, including debris removal, site preparation, construction materials, utility reconnections, and code compliance requirements," the statement read.
Police, meanwhile, are still looking into the cause of the Bald Range wildfire.
Penticton RCMP said in a statement this week that its investigators are part of a multi-agency effort to find out the fire's cause believed to have started in the afternoon hours of Friday, Aug. 7.
"The investigation remains ongoing," the statement said.

"Investigators are seeking to speak with anyone who may have witnessed suspicious activity or observed individuals, vehicles, or other actions in the vicinity of Princeton-Summerland Road and Bathville Road, including the Crump Recreation Site and Trout Creek Recreation Site."

Brian Callow's Summerland mushroom farm, What the Fungus, was also a casualty of the fire. The property that housed its operations is now strewn with twisted metal, burned vehicles and equipment and the skeletons of greenhouses.

The property, owned by his business partner whose tree-service business supplied the wood chips to grow the mushrooms, is still strewn with debris and they have yet to obtain a demolition permit, which requires a hazard assessment.
Callow said the District of Summerland has voted to reduce the cost of demolition permits, but the town's dump remains closed and "getting rid of all the waste seems to be a big issue right now."
He said the farm wasn't insured, but they've raised money in an online fundraiser and had offers of help from people in the community to replace lost tools and for materials to rebuild.

"But replacing all the specialized mushroom equipment, especially with the tariff war that's going on with the U.S. and Canada, all of our equipment comes from the U.S.," he said. "So, I don't even have a price of replacing that yet. It'll be quite expensive."

items: Homes across B.C. have been decimated by wildfires. Here's what to know about your insurance

blocks.text: The fire's behaviour, he said, was puzzling — but it ended up on multiple sides of the property, burning up vehicles and buildings.
An orange Kubota tractor stands out among the rubble, looking like it had been mostly spared by the flames, and Callow said it had been started and moved by firefighters.
"But by the time he got there it had already been half-melted — and believe it or not that's about $20,000 worth of damage on it," he said.
He said he'd been sent a video of the property engulfed in flames. He didn't even recognize it as he watched it burn.
'Everybody's forgotten us'

The destruction of Faulder and evacuation of thousands of people from Summerland were defining moments of B.C.'s wildfire season, playing out on videos and images that flooded social media and went around the world.
But earlier in the season, residents in and around Clinton in the Cariboo region also fled fires that merged into the Big Bar Complex of wildfires.
Steve and Kathy Naseth had lived in their modular home outside Clinton for 25 years, and after the evacuation order was lifted and Steve returned to begin the cleanup, "it was devastation."
"The problem I'm finding is I think everybody's forgotten about us," he said.
The couple has insurance, but they said they felt failed by the provincial and regional governments.
While the spotlight was on the evacuation of Summerland, they said those on the outskirts of Clinton haven't received attention despite being displaced after their homes were destroyed.

The couple, both in their early 60s, is staying in a trailer on their property, but they'll be staying in Cache Creek during the winter, and face years of rebuilding that has delayed their retirement plans.
Their son-in-law has been helping with cleanup, but they also have hectares of range lands that need to be refenced.
"We don't have the mobility or the machinery to do that and that's going to come out of our insurance, which is costly. It takes away from what we can put back into our home," Kathy said.

"We had a four-bedroom modular home. It was beautiful. Now we have to shrink it down to three, possibly even two, just to make sure we've got a roof over our head because we don't know where else to go.
"This was our retirement home and we were going to sell it and of course then go travelling."
She said they'll likely have to work for a few more years because of the loss, even with their insurance because it's not "going to be enough."

"We were here for 25 years," she said. "We don't have 25 years again to build that all up again, and we've lost photos, we've lost heirlooms, we've lost everything. And we're not the only ones, like the rest of this valley, they lost everything. Most of them don't have insurance. "

Louis and Shorty Fred's home on the Okanagan Indian Band reserve near Vernon, B.C., was destroyed in the Bradley Creek blaze in early August, and they're expecting a "long haul" as a phased recovery gets underway.
They said they got a chance to look at their property soon after the fire.
"There's not much to go through, it's just all ash and rubble right now," Shorty Fred said.
Louis Fred said there's still dangerous trees to be dealt with, and while the road is open and power lines are back up, the cleanup and environmental assessment will be "quite the process."
They said they don't plan to rebuild on the same part of their property, moving to a part that wasn't hit by the fire.
"It's going to be a while, but we're really fortunate," he said.
Louis Fred said he was diagnosed with cancer a few years ago, and a tumour the size a golf ball was found on his spine. He was on crutches for a while.
"I went through one heck of a time," he said.
They said their Christian faith helped them through the health scare, and they're relying on it to get them through the aftermath of the fire.

"You don't realize these things. It's the little things that we all take for granted nowadays. Until you lose it, then you realize like, hey, you've got to take a better look at your life and thank God," Shorty Fred said.

items: Investigators called in after multiple fires ignite in wildfire-ravaged Boston Bar

blocks.text: Louis Fred recalled not being able to eat during his cancer treatment and being grateful after a trip to A&W where he had "the best doggone Mama Burger I ever ate in my life. It tasted so good I was laughing and crying at the same time."
He said he turned 78 a week after the fire and believes "God cleaned the slate."

"We have a new opportunity to start over again and do it right this time. Do everything right," he said. "We feel bad about the things that we did lose that you can't replace, like all our pictures and stuff back from my grandma. But life goes on."

articles.title: How Bulgaria become a global leader in battery storage and what this means for the country's grid and energy market?
articles.summary: In under two years, Bulgaria has become one of the world's most battery-intensive energy markets. Can the surge last — and what will it mean for conventional power generators?

image.caption: Powerhouse in southeastern Europe: Bulgaria has one of the world's highest ratios of battery storage to total power capacity in the world. Pictured here: a solar park with storage batteries in Maglizh, BulgariaImage: Tsvetelina Belutova/Capital

blocks.text: The international energy sector currently has a curious case study in an unlikely place: Bulgaria, a country in southeastern Europe with a population of just 6.4 million, now has one of the world's highest ratios of battery storage to total power capacity, outpacing markets like California, Germany and China.

In less than two years, Bulgaria's battery storage capacity has gone from zero to making up nearly a quarter of the country's total installed power capacity, fueled by EU funding and private capital worth close to €3 billion ($3.4 billion), according to calculations by Bulgaria's leading business publication Capital.
Bulgaria was lucky enough to escape the worst of the heatwaves and droughts that forced a cut in nuclear and hydro output in Hungary and Romania this summer.
During that period, it turned its batteries into a key grid stabilizer for neighboring markets and profited by storing cheap solar power and selling it in the evening when prices spike.

blocks.caption: Bulgaria used its batteries this summer as a key grid stabilizer for neighboring marketsImage: imageBROKER/Nikola Spasov/imagebroker/IMAGO

blocks.text: And while experts say the Bulgarian battery boom went "under the radar," it remains to be seen how this rapid development will affect the other generators of power, whether the current business model is sustainable and whether private investment will dictate a shift in the national strategy for the country's energy transition.
What is the Bulgarian battery boom?
In January 2026, a report by the energy think tank Ember estimated Bulgaria's battery capacity — both operational and in the pipeline — to be 1.66 GW.
Eight months later, capacity had more than tripled to 5.4 GW, according to data from ENTSO-E. Bulgaria's Ministry of Energy told AFP it had already reached 5.7 GW.
"Two years ago, no one imagined we would have even half of this capacity," Ivaylo Stanchev, editor-in-chief of the business publication Capital, told DW.

Stanchev compiled one of the country's most comprehensive lists of battery projects, filling a gap left by the absence of an official public database. The list itself reflects investment levels that have outpaced official forecasts.

blocks.caption: Ivaylo Stanchev, editor-in-chief of the business publication Capital, says that Bulgaria having this kind of battery capacity was unimaginable just two years ago Image: Capital

blocks.text: While the rapid battery buildout was sparked by the Next Generation EU recovery fund and the subsequent RESTORE programs, which approved €700 million ($797 million) in funding for 113 projects, Stanchev estimates that private investment amounted to almost three times that figure: roughly €2 billion.
Although most of the lithium batteries come from China, the investors are mostly from Bulgaria or from other European countries, which see potential in the growing niche.
How much can the batteries store?

"When fully charged, the batteries can store enough energy to power the whole country for several hours," said Stanchev, drawing a comparison that, although practically impossible, illustrates the scale of the development.
Its effects are already tangible: Bulgaria produces a large amount of solar energy and buys more from Greece and Romania.

Daily prices during the summer tend to be low or even negative during the sunniest hours of the day, allowing batteries to buy cheap energy, store it and discharge it in the evening, when local and international markets need it, at a higher price.
The main export destination is Romania, which was particularly badly hit during the summer as it had to reduce nuclear capacity because of the drought along the Danube.
Bulgaria, historically a net exporter, has thus turned into a regional battery hub, with an operational storage capacity that is now greater than that of Greece and Romania combined.
What is the impact of this rapid development?

There is no measurement that isolates the batteries' specific electricity price contribution, but Bulgaria's average price fell relative to other countries in the region during the first summer of large-scale battery operation.
And while households in Bulgaria are subject to fixed electricity prices set by the state and have not yet seen a reduction in their electricity bills, industrial companies benefited from the change.

"Between August 1 and August 16, the average day-ahead electricity price per MWh in Bulgaria was €132.2 — almost €14 lower than the price in Romania, even though they used to be almost equal," said Stanchev, adding that the difference comes mainly from the evening hours where the batteries' effect is most at play.
Additionally, the batteries bring more security to the grid both domestically and regionally — as well as more revenue from exports and potential tax revenue from the company profits, he explained.

blocks.caption: It is estimated that approx. €700 million in EU funding and roughly €2 billion in private money have powered Bulgaria's battery storage boomImage: Tsvetelina Belutova/Capital

blocks.text: Yet, these effects are part of the summer period snapshot, raising questions about the sustainability of the model throughout the year.
Is this all good news?

"Such record development should always be taken with a pinch of salt," said Kaloyan Staykov, chair of the Management Board of the Energy Management Institute in Bulgaria, adding that the year-long effects of the vast battery buildout "are yet to be seen."
Staykov argues that, while a positive development for the market overall, the shift has come at a cost for conventional energy generators.

"While the electricity price during the evening peak is now down, the generation that used to be more profitable during those hours needs to make up for the lower revenue stream, which pushes up the baseload price," he said.

This issue points to a broader one. "Investments in batteries go beyond any national strategy for what the sector will look like in 10 or 20 years' time," he said, adding that "the role of national strategic roadmaps is changing from a leading one, to a following one."
This comes at a time when Bulgaria is slowly pursuing a transition away from coal, including the expected phase-out of coal mining.

At the same time, the country is advancing the rehabilitation of a massive pumped-storage hydropower plant (Chaira) and intends to build two new nuclear reactors at the Kozloduy Nuclear Power Plant in the years to come.
The rise in renewable energy and the risk of cannibalization
Between 2022 and 2026, photovoltaic buildout in Bulgaria more than quadrupled, according to data from ENTSO-E.

blocks.caption: Kaloyan Staykov of the Energy Management Institute in Bulgaria cautions that the year-long effects of the vast battery buildout 'are yet to be seen'Image: Maria Sabotinova

blocks.text: Private investors seized on the potential offered by this technology by building battery storage at solar parks and elsewhere — a development that was facilitated by the fact that it is in general easy to obtain permits for such batteries in Bulgaria.

Delyan Dobrev, a former MP and energy minister from the center-right GERB party who has recently stepped down from politics, announced in an interview with Focus news agency in September what he describes as advanced talks with US giant Tesla for an additional battery complex — one he says is expected to be among "the largest in Europe."

Yet Staykov warned that it remains to be seen how much more growth the market and grid can absorb in the short-term, as the system adjusts to this new reality and investors realize the first-mover advantage may already be shrinking.

As more batteries connect to the grid, revenue per unit can fall. Yet both Staykov and Stanchev agree that introducing ancillary services that allow batteries to discharge energy to stabilize the grid will be key in the future.
Such a development would be new for Bulgaria and might ease concerns about potential cannibalization, in other words batteries competing away their own margins as capacity grows.
"This year we managed to capitalize on the situation, although no one can predict what the markets will look like this autumn or in three years' time," said Staykov.
How batteries stabilize the power grid in northern Germany

articles.title: Iranian President Pezeshkian brought a diplomatic tone to New York for UNGA. What did his remarks signal?
articles.summary: Iran's president used his trip to New York this week for the UN General Assembly to signal openness to talks over the nuclear dispute. However, the chances of a major breakthrough on the war remain…

image.caption: Iranian President Masud Peseschkian addressed the UN General Assembly in New York while his country is at war with the USImage: Kyle Mazza/CNP/IMAGO

blocks.text: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, who travelled to New York to attend the UN General Assembly, met with American journalists and media representatives.
In an interview with the conservative US broadcaster Fox News, he signaled a willingness to make concessions in the nuclear dispute with the United States.

Washington has made clear that Iran must never be allowed to possess nuclear weapons. Asked whether Iran was prepared to hand over its highly enriched uranium, Pezeshkian said his country would comply with its obligationsunder international law and the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty.
In its most recent assessment, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), estimated that Iran had more than 440 kilograms of uranium enriched to up to 60%.

Since the US-Israeli attacks on Iranian nuclear facilities in 2025, Iran suspended its cooperation with the IAEA. The agency has continued to demand access to Iranian facilities and updated information on its nuclear stockpile and the whereabouts of its nuclear material.
Asked point-blank "Do you want a nuclear bomb or not?" during the exclusive interview on Fox News' "Special Report," Pezeshkian firmly rejected the premise.

"Not at all. Not at all. Our martyred, esteemed supreme leader had announced several times that, from a religious decree, it is unholy. It is illegal," he told Bret Baier, referencing religious edicts issued against weapons of mass destruction.
Despite Pezeshkians claims, the IAEA has assessed that Iran's fissile material is being enriched far beyond what is needed for civilian use.
Trump threatens to 'annihilate' Iran if no deal is reached
Diplomacy: A first step?

A major breakthrough in the conflict between Iran and the United States is not expected anytime soon, Iran expert Arman Mahmoudian, a lecturer in Middle East Studies at the University of South Florida, told DW.

"Pezeshkian does not have the authority to initiate comprehensive de-escalation with the United States. In particular, hardliners and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) appear to continue to wield considerable influence over Iran's decision-making process," he added.
Nevertheless, Mahmoudian thinks Pezeshkian's visit could help establish a more direct channel of communication between Tehran and Washington.

He also sees the possibility of creating a framework for future negotiations in New York, adding that the two sides could develop a roadmap that would pave the way for more substantive talks and, in the longer term, potentially contribute to de-escalation.

There are already signs of this, including meetings between Iranian and US delegations earlier this week. The White House, meanwhile, confirmed that "positive and constructive" talks were continuing through intermediaries.
Hormuz — and Houthis — as leverage

The future of the Strait of Hormuz is also at the center of the discussions. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi reportedly said that Tehran had presented Washington with a proposal to resume negotiations.
Under the proposal, the strategically important waterway could be reopened within seven days if certain conditions were met. It remains unclear what those conditions are.

In the past, Iran has demanded the release of frozen Iranian assets, an end to the US blockade of Iranian ports and vessels, and a commitment by Washington not to interfere in Iran's internal affairs.
Strike on Iran school: Did US commit a war crime?
The Strait of Hormuz, through which around 20 million barrels of oil normally pass every day — roughly 20% of global oil consumption — has become one of Iran's most important sources of leverage.
The United States has failed to eliminate all of Iran's capabilities to threaten shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, Kelly Grieco, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center, told DW in July.
This is despite the US attacks having caused significant damage to Iran's navy and defense industry.
"At a certain point, it becomes really hard to find some of these targets," said Grieco. "They're mobile. They're distributed."

Without a long-term strategy, Grieco warned, the United States could therefore become trapped in a recurring cycle: Iran rebuilds its military capabilities, Washington launches another round of attacks, and the cycle repeats itself.
Nearly seven months after the start of the Iran war, the conflict has also spread to a second strategically important shipping route.

The Iran-backed Houthi movement has expanded its control over Yemen's Red Sea coast and the strategically important area around the Bab al-Mandab Strait. This gives Iran another important lever along major international shipping routes.
Balancing pressure and negotiations

Mahmoudian expects Iran to continue pursuing a dual strategy of military pressure and diplomacy, saying that Tehran is likely to continue using the Strait of Hormuz as leverage and to prevent a full return to normal shipping traffic.
Red Sea strains rattle energy markets

"At the same time, Iran will most likely continue rebuilding its military and strategic infrastructure inside the country," he said. "Reports suggest that Iranian authorities are already moving quickly to reconstruct some damaged facilities."
On the diplomatic front, he added that Iran is likely to continue negotiations with the US, either directly or through intermediaries.

Tehran is aware that the current situation, with the continuing threat of military attacks, sanctions and economic pressure, is not sustainable in the long term, Mahmoudian said, adding that Iran will therefore continue to have an interest in reaching a political agreement with Washington.

A deal with Iran will require time and difficult negotiations, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in New York on September 23, playing down expectations of a quick agreement. At the same time, he stressed that President Donald Trump has military options at his disposal alongside the diplomatic route.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: After Xi-Trump summit, US-China rivalry remains frozen. Is this to Beijing's advantage?
articles.summary: The US president showcased White House construction projects and hosted a lavish dinner with tech CEOs, but the summit made little progress on key issues such as trade tensions and AI regulation.

image.caption: Chinese leader Xi Jinping was treated to a personal tour of the US presidential helicopterImage: Evan Vucci/REUTERS

blocks.text: When US President Donald Trump rolled out the red carpet for Chinese leader Xi Jinping at Andrews Air Force Base on Wednesday evening, it was a rare diplomatic gesture that has only happened a handful of times in US history.

Generally, world leaders are received by the president at the White House. Xi's VIP reception underlines the importance Trump places on his personal rapport with China's most powerful leader in a generation.

blocks.caption: The last US president to greet a world leader at Andrews Air Force Base was John F. Kennedy in 1962Image: Alex Brandon/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: After 90 minutes of bilateral talks in the Oval Office, Trump spent Thursday afternoon showing his "good friend" Xi his various White House construction projects, including the helipad completed just days earlier over the South Lawn. He then welcomed Xi aboard the presidential helicopter Marine One for a brief tour.
Trump's 'personal diplomacy'
Trump then told reporters "we had a great meeting," adding that Xi "loves good granite."

The optics continued at a glitzy state dinner Thursday night, where Trump said he and President Xi have "never gotten along better" and lauded building a "relationship that promotes prosperity and security for future generations."

Judging from Xi's mannerisms, it isn't clear the Chinese leader shares Trump's enthusiasm for personal diplomacy. When Trump arrived in Beijing for a summit in May, Xi sent diplomatic envoy, Vice President Han Zheng, to meet the US president.

"Trump's 'personalized diplomacy' is a one-sided construct — one that exists mainly in his own mind. He may believe his personal rapport with Xi is the key factor shaping Sino-American relations, but there's little to no evidence backing that claim," said Aurelio Insisa, senior analyst at the Berlin-based Mercator Institute for China Studies (MERICS).
Xi's whirlwind visit to the US, his first in 10 years, has been heavy on pomp, but relatively low on substance.

As of Friday morning, most summit coverage has focused on what was for dinner and the tech CEO guest list, in lieu of any deliverables on thorny issues like trade deals or cooperation on artificial intelligence. There is still time for announcements when Xi departs Washington later Friday after visiting the National Archives with Trump.
"The Chinese approach has shown no meaningful deviation in the US President's favor, beneath the usual pomp and circumstance of apex-level summitry," Insisa told DW.

blocks.caption: Showing off his new helipad, Trump said Xi is an 'expert on stone' Image: Evan Vucci/REUTERS

blocks.text: Trade truce extended, rare earths a quesiton mark
The most-pressing issue remains managing a trade war launched by Trump's scattershot tariffs in April 2025 that at one point were so high they essentially amounted to an embargo on Chinese goods.

On Wednesday, US Treasury Secretary Bessent said a trade truce due to expire in November would be extended until January "to give us more time to see what we can do on the economic front." Such an extension had been widely expected before the summit.

The trade truce builds on the "Busan deal" Trump and Xi agreed on at a meeting in South Korea last October, where Trump backed off on more tariffs in exchange for Xi easing export control for rare earths, which are critical ingredients for building high-tech kit.
Levering China's chokehold on rare earths to confront Trump's tariff blitz represented a major victory for Xi.

The Financial Times reported earlier this week that the US "believes China has not fully lived up to its commitment of uninterrupted supply," adding that China's shipments of rare earths to the US have dropped recently, amid concerns China could again "choke supplies."
What to expect from the Trump-Xi summit?

On tariffs and trade, Trump made nebulous comments on Thursday about "progress," but no specific deals on sectors or goods have yet been reported as of Friday morning. Reports ahead of the summit of an expected $30 billion in two-way tariff cuts have also yet to be proven.

Melanie Hart, director of Global China Hub at the Atlantic Council, wrote in a briefing earlier this week that the tariff cut announcement has been "so widely expected that if it is derailed, it will indicate something has gone horribly wrong."

Agreements and negotiations are happening through the US-China "Board of Trade," which was announced in May. US trade representative Jamieson Greer has said the board is operating, with initial lists of possible products including US agricultural goods and Chinese LNG and low-tech goods.
China also wants more access to cutting-edge chips made by US companies needed to develop frontier AI models.

Also unresolved is the question of US secondary sanctions targeting Iran's financiers,which would include Chinese banks. Trump has also dismissed reports China provided targeting intelligence to Iran.
"The foundations of this trade truce are brittle, and it will likely not survive the end of the second Trump presidency," Insisa said.

"Beijing will not radically alter its industrial and trade policy to meet Washington's demands, and future US administrations — even Republican ones — will likely deviate from Trump's approach to China."
Talk but no walk on AI
Following safety warnings from AI labs, AI regulation and the US-China tech race were thrust into the spotlight ahead of the summit, but expectations for true cooperation are low.

On Sunday, a US-China AI "dialogue" was announced after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and trade representative Greer met with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng. Other items included a possible crisis communications line. It is unclear when the group will meet again, with the APEC summit in November providing a possible venue.
How US, China could end the AI race
Trump sees developing AI as a winner-take-all race to the top, and has also reduced the incentive for China to slow down its own development, having called the AI lab's safety warnings a "hoax."

Further complicating any parallel AI regulatory frameworks between the US and China is a lack of trust or transparency, where it is impossible to verify if one side is complying with agreed-upon rules. There are also diverging ideas on what regulation means, according to MERICS analyst Antonia Hmaidi.
Xi's ask on Taiwan
Almost every Trump-Xi summit has been overshadowed by fears that the transactional US president will trade in supporting the self-ruled democracy Taiwan for a deal with Beijing.

This has been compounded by Trump having delayed a $14 billion (€12.2 billion) US arms package for Taiwan passed by Congress in January. Following the May summit, Trump called the package a "good bargaining chip."
Beijing claims Taiwan as Chinese territory and has vowed to crush any attempts at "independence."

But despite these fears, the US under Trump has yet to shift its narrative on Taiwan, maintaining a posture of "strategic ambiguity" by providing defense support but not officially taking a position on Taiwanese sovereignty.
This creates a delicate diplomatic balance based on language.

Chinese state media reported Xi told Trump he hopes the US will "adhere to the correct position of opposing 'Taiwan independence." If Trump accepted "opposition," it would represent a major break from the current, more passive, formulation of "not supporting" independence.
Trump's off-the-cuff communication style has led to concerns an errant utterance could be interpreted as a change in position, but this has yet to happen.
Freezing the US-China rivalry

By holding summit after summit building on positive superficial optics, Beijing is maintaining what Chinese policymakers have recently begun calling "constructive strategic stability" in its multifront competition with the US.
"The summit is evidence that the current trajectory in the bilateral relationship continues to favor China," said MERICS analyst Insisa.

blocks.caption: Tech CEOs joined the leaders of the US and China for a state dinner at the White House Image: Alex Brandon/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: At the White House dinner, Xi's statement echoed similar remarks made during May's state dinner in Beijing.

"President Trump has pledged to make America great again ... China is committed to achieving great national rejuvenation ... These two goals are both ambitious and can surely be mutually reinforcing," Xi said.

But Xi's Trump-aligned rhetoric belies what Beijing sees as a fading US-led world order, or what it calls "great changes unseen in a century." While Trump is focused on US midterm elections in November, Xi has his eye on securing another five years at the helm during next year's CCP national congress.

"China has perfected its 'Trump playbook' since his return to power and the tariff spat triggered by his 'Liberation Day' announcement in April 2025," Insisa said. "For the time being, Beijing has found a way to keep the Trump administration engaged while avoiding concrete steps on the most pressing issues: AI governance, trade relations, export controls," he added.
The next time the two leaders are expected to meet will be on the sidelines of November's APEC summit in Shenzhen. These issues will most likely all still be on the table, and Xi can wait.
Trump hosts China's Xi for state visit

articles.title: Meloni accused of election shift to right after ’shameful’ cap on foreign children in classrooms
articles.summary:
Critics say decree also banning burqa in schools shows Italian PM running scared ahead of next year’s vote

Rights campaigners have accused the Italian government of ramping up divisive…
articles.byline: Ashifa Kassam European community affairs correspondent

blocks.text: Rights campaigners have accused the Italian government of ramping up divisive rhetoric in an attempt to court far-right voters ahead of next year’s general election after it passed a decree aimed at capping the number of newly arrived migrants in classrooms and banning the burqa and niqab in schools.

The prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, who leads the far-right Brothers of Italy party, said her government had approved what she called “commonsense measures that do not divide but genuinely help to integrate”.
Writing on social media, she added: “A limit of 30% in classrooms for students who do not adequately know Italian, plus tools to learn our language and a halt to burqas and niqabs in school.”

The announcement was a toned-down version of comments she had made earlier in the week at an event organised by Brothers of Italy’s youth division. “It cannot be that in the classroom it is Italian children who feel left out because they’ve become the minority,” Meloni said as she vowed to “legally set the number of foreign students per class”.

Thursday’s decree also sets out that in cases where students show persistent problems with integrating or struggle to learn the language, their parents will be referred to social services and will have to take free literacy and Italian language classes. Failure to comply on the part of parents could result in fines of up to €1,000.
The education minister, Giuseppe Valditara, said the measures, set to take effect in the 2027-28 school year, would affect about 1,000 classrooms, or about 0.3% of the total nationwide.
Rights campaigners were swift to link the measures to next year’s election, in which Meloni’s premiership is facing an unexpected challenger on the right.

“She’s creating an emergency that is not a real emergency at all,” said Daniela Ionita, of the campaign group Italians without Citizenship, pointing out that an estimated 60% of the pupils who could be described as foreign were born in Italy but faced a myriad of hurdles when it came to accessing citizenship. “Because there are now new parties pushing from the right, I think Meloni is scared,” she said.

blocks.caption: Jannatur Nayeem, 33, an Italian citizen of Bangladeshi origin, chats with other mothers as they wait for a sports session to end at a school in Rome on Thursday. Photograph: Alessandra Tarantino/AP

blocks.text: The government said students born and raised in Italy or who had attended at least two years of nursery school or completed three years of schooling in Italy would be exempt from the measures.

Ionita said the ramped-up rhetoric was an attempt by the government to mask how little it had accomplished during its time in power. “If you remove every decree linked to security or to migrants, the government’s political and economic programme will fall apart, and very little concrete remains of one of the longest-serving governments of the last years in Italy,” she said.

Marco Tarchi, a political scientist who focuses on the extreme right and teaches at the University of Florence, said the school measures were “undoubtedly” driven by fears of a new political challenge on the right.
Since February, a new party, Futuro Nazionale (FN), has galvanised the extreme right, with polls suggesting it could capture about 8% of the vote in an election expected as early as spring 2027.

Led by Roberto Vannacci, a former army general best known for self-publishing a book rife with racism, homophobia, Islamophobia and antisemitism, the party’s popularity in polls has eclipsed that of Brothers of Italy’s two coalition partners, the League and the conservative Forza Italia.

blocks.caption: Roberto Vannacci’s party Futuro Nazionale has galvanised the extreme right. Photograph: Remo Casilli/Reuters

blocks.text: Those who have shifted allegiances include some who had enthusiastically lined up behind Meloni years ago as she spoke of “ethnic substitution” and vowed to install an all-out naval blockade to prevent migrant arrivals from north Africa.

Tarchi said: “Many of the FN’s potential voters are former supporters of Giorgia Meloni’s party who are disappointed that, once in power, the leader softened many of her previous stances regarding the European Union, which she had harshly criticised; immigration, on which she had made radical proposals that were later abandoned; and other issues.”

He said Vannacci had capitalised on this, capturing voters with an extreme manifesto that promised “remigration” and limits on the number of foreigners in the country, as well as curtailing LGBTQ+ rights and negating the right to abortion. He said that in order to win back this support, Meloni could have to adopt positions closer to those she held while in opposition.

A glimpse of what this could look like came this summer when Meloni seized on the sudden entry of tens of thousands of people into the tiny Spanish territory of Ceuta in north Africa, said Elisa De Pieri, a researcher at Amnesty International.

“Meloni immediately exploited the situation in Ceuta, which had absolutely nothing to do with Italy and nothing to do with the Schengen space, but she made it into a supposed crisis for Italy,” she said. “And so that’s the mode that I think we’re going to see in the next months.”

De Pieri predicted that Meloni “won’t be talking too much” about Italy’s offshore detention agreement with Albania on the grounds that it had not been successful as she would have hoped. “It’s been very costly, and it’s been struck down repeatedly by national and international courts,” she said.

blocks.caption: A reception camp for migrants transferred from Italy in Gjader, Albania, in 2024. Photograph: Florion Goga/Reuters

blocks.text: Instead, she expects that Meloni will adopt a more aggressive tone on migration more generally, leading to a polarising electoral campaign whose impact would be disproportionately borne among migrant communities.

The view was echoed by critics of the new measures who pointed out the rarity of burqas or niqabs in Italian classrooms and said the government was simply repackaging previous, unenforced policies, given that the 30% threshold was previously floated by the education ministry in 2010. Save the Children said the overall impact would be to “create ‘first-class’ and ‘second-class’ students”.

The leader of the Democratic party, Elly Schlein, described the decree as “shameful” and accused the government of “living on a different planet”. She said Italian parents were grappling with a very different set of issues, citing crumbling school buildings, the high costs of textbooks and low salaries of teachers.

“Faced with all this, the government’s response is to kick foreign children out of the classroom,” Schlein said. “Who do they think they’re kidding? After four years of cuts and no serious investment in school buildings, they’re inventing a witch-hunt that targets the youngest children.”
